title: FilmTogether: Cinematic Video Generation from Low-Cost Inputs
shortTitle: FilmTogether: Cinematic Video Generation from Low-Cost Inputs
abstract: The widespread adoption of mobile devices has democratized video recording, but a stark aesthetic divide persists between casual, low-cost captures and high-cost cinematic productions. Bridging this gap requires upgrading heterogeneous production elements, such as lighting, specialized costumes, and materials, without altering the core layout, identity, and temporal motion of the original footage. However, this task is heavily bottlenecked by two important challenges: 1) Lacking a high-quality paired training data specifically designed to handle complex low-to-high appearance shifts. 2) Ignoring the capacity of current video editing models to perceive and enhance the multiple low-cost compositions. To address these issues, we present CineCraft-120K, a large-scale dataset of aligned low- and high-cost video pairs annotated with pair-aware editing prompts. CineCraft-120K features a diverse, high-resolution and high-cost Cinematic Crafting bank spanning decades of media production, meticulously taxonomized into 5 broad domains and 23 fine-grained sub-categories. It also provides element-level mapping between low- and high-cost counterparts, offering pair-aware rich textual prompts that precisely detail the required aesthetic transformations while anchoring structural layout. Architecturally, we propose a simple yet effective dual-memory feature adapter, where a text-memory expands semantic capacity for low2high appearance changes, and a hint memory supplies layer-wise visual feature corrections of high-cost element before context injection. Extensive experiments and ablation studies demonstrate the superiority of CineCraft-120K for low-to-high-cost video editing, alongside the effectiveness of our dual-memory adapter.

title: Benchmarking Machine-Learning Classifiers for Neoantigen Immunogenicity Prediction and the Limits of SHAP Interpretability
shortTitle: Benchmarking Machine-Learning Classifiers for Neoantigen Immunogenicity Prediction and the Limits of SHAP Interpretability
abstract: Personalized cancer vaccines require prioritizing, among hundreds of candidate mutant peptides, the few that will induce a T-cell response. This study asks what general-purpose machine learning achieves on that task, and whether the features such models identify as important can be trusted. We make three contributions. The first is a benchmark of sixty models: twelve supervised classifier families, each in five configurations, evaluated on the Immunogenic Tumor Specific Neoantigen database (ITSNdb; 199 experimentally validated neoantigens, 129 immunogenic and 70 non-immunogenic). All sixty are compared under one stratified k-fold cross-validation protocol, in which the data used to choose a configuration are never the data used to score it. The second is an interpretability study that combines SHAP with feature ablation. The third is a shuffled-label control that tests whether a SHAP value has been earned. Two results follow, and both run against current practice. First, the classical linear models lead the ranking. The gradient-boosted ensembles and neural networks that dominate recent work bring no advantage. Second, SHAP can fail on high-cardinality categorical features. Ablation establishes the presenting HLA allele as the dominant input and the source gene as dispensable. SHAP reports the opposite, assigning 68.7% to 81.7% of its total value to the source gene in every model that gives each gene its own weight. Shuffling the gene labels at random among the peptides resolves the contradiction: the meaningless column earns the same SHAP value as the real one. That value measures only that ITSNdb contains 173 genes for 199 peptides. We therefore recommend that SHAP values for high-cardinality categorical annotations in cohorts of this size always be reported against such a shuffled-label control, and we describe one in full.

title: ZOPGA-KD: Zeroth Order PGA Guided Data Free Knowledge Distillation
shortTitle: ZOPGA-KD: Zeroth Order PGA Guided Data Free Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) enables the transfer of learned representations from a large teacher network to a small student network. In foundational KD, the student network uses the original training data of the teacher model to accomplish this task. However, due to privacy concerns, the original training data is often not available. To overcome this reliance on original training data, several data-free knowledge distillation methods have been developed. Some of these methods operate in the white-box setting, and a few methods generate synthetic data by training a generator network. White-box methods use the teacher model's parameters to obtain a synthetic dataset. To avoid relying on teacher parameters, some methods use computationally expensive generative approaches to obtain such a dataset. There also exist certain black-box methods that generate the synthetic data without accessing teacher parameters. These methods are also computationally intensive. We propose a data-free knowledge distillation method that utilizes just the teacher's output logits and does not require access to its architecture, parameters, or gradients. We generate synthetic data via Projected Gradient Ascent (PGA) starting from smooth random noise signals. Required gradients are obtained through zeroth-order gradient estimation rather than backpropagating through the teacher's parameters. The student is then trained on these synthetically generated samples. We evaluate the proposed method on several benchmark datasets and show that the distillation performance is comparable with approaches that have access to the teacher model parameters.

title: S1CogBench: What System One Decision Models Can and Cannot Do on Cognitive Experiments
shortTitle: S1CogBench: What System One Decision Models Can and Cannot Do on Cognitive Experiments
abstract: Language models are no longer used only to generate text. Software also asks them for decisions, in routing, guardrails, and automated gates. System One decision models, also called typed decision models, such as Jev and Laya, return one fast decision over the legal options, leaving no text to inspect. However, a fast, well-formed decision does not show that the model used the evidence. Cognitive experiments can test this, because they vary task demands and measure how behavior changes, yet existing cognitive benchmarks evaluate language and multimodal models. We introduce S1CogBench to ask what these models can and cannot do on 24 cognitive tasks, evaluating five open models and Jev and keeping conditions and scoring apart from disclosed adaptations. We find that decision models vary widely in reliability, acting well does not imply predicting humans, aggregate scores hide how decisions respond to conditions, and speed comes mainly from answering without generation. To our knowledge, S1CogBench is the first benchmark of System One decision models on established cognitive experiments, and it gives a shared test of whether their decisions respond to evidence, feedback, memory load, and future opportunities before software relies on them.

title: Elastic Precision: Software-Hardware Co-Design of a Mixed-Precision Architecture for Long-Context LLM Inference
shortTitle: Elastic Precision: Software-Hardware Co-Design of a Mixed-Precision Architecture for Long-Context LLM Inference
abstract: Low-bit quantization reduces the data movement and computation costs of large language model (LLM) inference, but uniform widths can waste precision and degrade model quality. Existing mixed-precision methods do not fully account for how the other input of the current GEMM tile affects output error when selecting one input's width. Using both inputs to guide precision introduces additional estimation and selection overheads on conventional hardware. We propose Coffee, a runtime precision allocation architecture for long-context LLM inference. Under a fixed average bit-width budget, Coffee combines statistics from both current input matrices to estimate output errors at candidate widths and select each subarray's two input widths, allocating more bits where they yield greater estimated error reductions. Its mixed-precision hardware supports the selected widths in data access and computation, while overlapping error estimation and width selection with transfers and computation to limit stalls. The same read path supports attention-guided KV reads during decoding, reducing memory traffic. Coffee achieves lower perplexity and higher average zero-shot accuracy than the evaluated quantization baselines, and higher long-context retrieval recall than PLENA. For long-context decoding, system modeling projects up to $2.55\times$ the throughput and $2.61\times$ the energy efficiency of the reconfigured PLENA baseline, and up to $4.96\times$ and $12.56\times$, respectively, compared with the B200 GPU baseline.

title: Benchmarking Classical Machine Learning Models for Shading-Fault Detection in Rooftop Photovoltaic Systems Using Real Sensor Data
shortTitle: Benchmarking Classical Machine Learning Models for Shading-Fault Detection in Rooftop Photovoltaic Systems Using Real Sensor Data
abstract: Most published comparisons of machine-learning classifiers for photovoltaic (PV) fault detection are validated on simulated faults. We compare seven classical and ensemble-tree classifiers on the Réunion dataset, a 4 kW domestic rooftop plant on which shading faults were physically staged and logged. Readings within a staged episode are near-duplicates, so every train/test split is grouped by episode. A 20,800-row subsample that retains all 17 fault episodes was evaluated with three repeats of five-fold group-aware nested cross-validation, with synthetic minority oversampling (SMOTE) applied inside the training folds. Random Forest and XGBoost gave the highest mean accuracy (0.838 and 0.831) and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC; 0.526 and 0.522). After Holm correction across the 21 pairwise Wilcoxon tests, only Random Forest's accuracy advantage over k-nearest neighbours and the multi-layer perceptron remained significant. Logistic Regression and the Decision Tree (accuracy 0.820) could be separated neither from the ensembles nor from the weakest models. SMOTE lowered binary MCC for six of the seven classifiers. Errors were concentrated in whole episodes: the Random Forest almost entirely missed four of the 17 fault episodes, including one of two uniform-shading and two of five intermittent-shading episodes. A post-hoc diagnostic shows that the no-fault rows were sampled over a wider range of times of day and output levels than the fault rows. Clock time alone reaches an MCC of 0.44, and PV-side voltage alone 0.72. The reported scores therefore reflect operating-condition differences as well as shading signatures. We release the pipeline and the diagnostics, and identify matched no-fault sampling as the step needed before the classifier ranking can be generalised.

title: TreePIN$^{2}$: Tree-Prior Initialized Neural Networks
shortTitle: TreePIN$^{2}$: Tree-Prior Initialized Neural Networks
abstract: Fitted decision trees provide predictive knowledge for neural network initialization. We present Tree-Prior Initialized Neural Networks (TreePIN$^{2}$), a method that translates split rules, decision paths and leaf predictions into initial network weights and biases for classification and regression. Sigmoid units encode split responses, hidden units combine them along decision paths, and leaf predictions initialize the output layer. We calibrate split softness using local training margins, sample support and impurity reduction, relating the initial responses to the data at each node. All weights and biases remain trainable, allowing gradient-based optimization to refine the transferred decisions and their combinations. Across six classification and six regression tasks with twenty paired seeds, TreePIN$^{2}$ improves mean initial and early validation performance over initialization baselines on most tasks. After fifty epochs, it achieves the best or tied-best mean validation performance among the six compared methods on ten tasks. Paired ablations show how split calibration and leaf-informed output initialization contribute to the starting predictor and its subsequent learning.

title: What matters in classical machine learning for non-intrusive load monitoring? A factorial benchmark on REFIT with validation on unseen houses
shortTitle: What matters in classical machine learning for non-intrusive load monitoring? A factorial benchmark on REFIT with validation on unseen houses
abstract: Published classical machine-learning results for appliance ON/OFF classification in nonintrusive load monitoring (NILM) range from F1-type scores of 0.53 to 0.98, and the sources of this spread have not been separated. This study separates them with a factorial benchmark on REFIT: seven models, two feature sets and four class-imbalance strategies for five appliances (270 fitted configurations), each evaluated by pooled nested cross-validation and on houses unseen during training, with robustness checks. An analysis of variance shows that the appliance explains 38% of the variance in F1, the feature set 13% and the model only 8%. Engineered rolling-window features raised the mean F1 score by 52% under both protocols. Other conclusions changed on unseen houses: the support-weighted F1 score of the best pooled configurations fell from 0.548 to 0.447, the differences between the models selected by pooled validation were no longer significant, and the benefit of class weighting over no correction rose from 32% to 69%. In a nested comparison, house-grouped selection on the training houses improved F1 on unseen houses for three of five appliances, by up to 0.110, and was within 0.007 for the other two. These findings held across four house partitions and without the solar-affected houses. A same-protocol convolutional network reached a weighted F1 score of 0.50, about 0.05 above the classical models (0.45) and far below the published deep-learning scores of 0.78 to 0.91, which were obtained under a different protocol. The results support low-cost appliance monitoring in buildings and yield a NILM reporting checklist.

title: Solvable dynamics model of in-context learning
shortTitle: Solvable dynamics model of in-context learning
abstract: Pretrained Transformer architectures display a surprising in-context learning ability without additional training. How the learning process guides the network to achieve this intriguing capability remains unsolved. In this study, we focus on a single-layer, single-head linear attention model, where empirical risk minimization is defined for learning. Given a finite amount of training examples, we determine the exact solution of network parameter dynamics, which is linked to the training error and generalization error, characterizing how memorization and generalization emerge from learning and how these transitions are related to curvatures of the empirical risk landscape. Furthermore, we calculate a data-dependent free energy, from which the training and generalization errors in the long-time limit of learning dynamics can be well predicted. Our work adds insights toward understanding the mechanism of in-context learning, especially from a learning dynamics perspective.

title: Illusion: Safeguarding Topology Confidentiality in LLM Multi-Agent Systems via Behavior-Preserving Obfuscation
shortTitle: Illusion: Safeguarding Topology Confidentiality in LLM Multi-Agent Systems via Behavior-Preserving Obfuscation
abstract: The communication topology of Large Language Model Multi-Agent Systems (LLM-MASs) governs how information propagates among agents and encodes critical domain knowledge and expert workflow design. It is valuable intellectual property and plays a decisive role in system utility and safety, yet remains vulnerable to inference attacks that stealthily reconstruct it from agent outputs. Existing defenses detect or mitigate such attacks but do not proactively conceal the topology itself. We propose \textit{Illusion}, a proactive topology obfuscation defense for LLM-MAS. \textit{Illusion} injects fake edges and fake messages to present attackers with a deceptive topology, while selecting low-impact candidates that preserve output-distribution equivalence and task-accuracy non-inferiority. The resulting fake edges are designed to be indistinguishable from genuine messages under black-box observation. Extensive experiments show that \textit{Illusion} reduces edge-level F1 from over 0.87 to 0.62 and graph similarity from over 0.94 to 0.71. It also largely preserves output distributions and task performance, and its fake edges resist both similarity-based and LLM-judge filtering, even under adaptive pruning.

title: UI-UG 2: Advancing Mobile UI Understanding and Generation with Fine-Grained Supervision and Reinforcement Learning
shortTitle: UI-UG 2: Advancing Mobile UI Understanding and Generation with Fine-Grained Supervision and Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Mobile UI understanding and generation require both fine-grained component perception and reliable structured synthesis. Inspired by the unified direction introduced by UI-UG, we present UI-UG 2, a compact 4B-parameter multimodal large language model (MLLM) that advances mobile UI Understanding and Generation with broader task coverage, a front-end-aligned taxonomy, and online render-aware reinforcement learning. UI-UG 2 constructs a multi-source understanding corpus from RICO, VINS, Android in the Wild, and Android Control, annotated with an 80-category two-level UI taxonomy aligned with front-end component semantics, and pairs it with over 5,000 requirement-screenshot-JSON tuples for progressive structured UI generation through a domain-specific language (DSL). For understanding, UI-UG 2 introduces decomposed rewards for category prediction, OCR fidelity, color recognition, dense grounding, and GUI grounding. Unlike the offline Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)-style generation optimization in UI-UG, UI-UG 2 optimizes generation through end-to-end online Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO): sampled DSL outputs are rendered with a Playwright-based server-side pipeline and evaluated using LLM-as-a-Judge and contrastive preference ranking. Experiments show that UI-UG 2 achieves the strongest referring and dense-grounding results among the evaluated models on our 80-category benchmark, and achieves the best composite generation score among compared models at a compact scale (4B). More importantly, we observe a consistent understanding-to-generation transfer: adding fine-grained UI perception supervision improves generation quality under a fixed training budget, suggesting that component-level semantics provide a shared representational foundation for both tasks.

title: Labadain-MedQA: A Tetun Medical QA Dataset for Fine-Tuning and Evaluating Large Language Models
shortTitle: Labadain-MedQA: A Tetun Medical QA Dataset for Fine-Tuning and Evaluating Large Language Models
abstract: Advances in large language models (LLMs) have created opportunities for cross-lingual transfer of medical knowledge from high-resource to low-resource languages to support access to healthcare information. However, medical question-answering (QA) datasets for fine-tuning and evaluating LLMs remain scarce for Tetun. To address this gap, we translated MedAlpaca's Medical Flashcards and WikiDoc Patient Information collections into Tetun using Gemini 2.5 Flash, producing 39,077 medical QA pairs. Translation quality was assessed on 50 randomly sampled QA pairs (100 documents) using automatic metrics against human reference translations and evaluations by two native Tetun-speaking healthcare professionals, focusing on medical accuracy and Tetun fluency. Human translations achieved higher mean ratings than LLM-generated translations for both criteria (4.43/5 vs. 4.02/5), with statistically significant differences (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.001). To assess downstream utility, we fine-tuned Gemma and Llama variants on the translated MedAlpaca dataset using parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) and evaluated them on 325 Tetun-translated United States Medical Licensing Examination multiple-choice questions. Gemma 4 12B fine-tuned using QLoRA achieved relative improvements in mean accuracy of 10.79% with 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) inference and 10.42% after merging the LoRA adapters into the BF16 base model, compared with the corresponding base models. These results highlight the viability of automatic dataset translation for Tetun medical QA and the effectiveness of PEFT in enhancing model performance. The datasets, models, and evaluation resources are accessible at https://github.com/labadain/labadain-medqa to support reproducible research on Tetun medical QA and facilitate machine translation, cross lingual, and multilingual research.

title: What Helps Denoising Can Hurt Memory: Rethinking History in Long Video Generation
shortTitle: What Helps Denoising Can Hurt Memory: Rethinking History in Long Video Generation
abstract: Autoregressive video generators produce long videos block by block, using historical context to maintain temporal consistency. After denoising, a committing pass encodes each clean block into keys and values (KV) that later blocks read, and the same clean block can be encoded into different KV depending on the history it reads. We therefore study historical context not only as a condition for denoising but also as an input to committing. Older historical context that supports denoising can harm subsequent generation when read during committing. At fixed context size and temporal positions, older historical context lowers mean clip-to-clip Subject Consistency. Across 5 generator configurations supporting longer contexts, consistency rises, plateaus, and then declines as committing context expands. Motivated by these findings, we propose Commit Forcing, a training-free rule that organizes committing into a chain. During committing, each block reads only the preceding block's stored KV, so older historical context reaches new entries only through the chain. We apply this rule to 6 pretrained generators. On 60-second VBench, Commit Forcing improves Quality and Total on all 6 generators, by up to 1.27 Quality points and 1.10 Total points. Long-range consistency gains extend to 240-second videos. In a blinded comparison on 120-second LongLive videos, Commit Forcing achieves win rates of 83.5% for subject and scene consistency and 82.9% for overall preference against the base generator, excluding ties.

title: Reformulation and Equivalence of Bock's Algorithm for Exact Dependency Parsing
shortTitle: Reformulation and Equivalence of Bock's Algorithm for Exact Dependency Parsing
abstract: Bock's algorithm provides a matrix-based alternative to Chu--Liu/Edmonds (CL/E) for exact dependency parsing. We present a reformulation that retains original node and arc identities through component labels, column adjustments, and star-and-bar transfers. In exact arithmetic, we prove operational equivalence to original Bock under matching scan and tie rules, and establish correspondence with corrected Tarjan under a prescribed component schedule. A separate analysis establishes optimal-value equivalence with Dozat-derived CL/E under the stated score and single-root conventions. We integrate reformulated Bock into a biaffine dependency parser and evaluate decoding and structured training on the Penn Treebank and Chinese Treebank. These results establish Bock as an alternative exact oracle for dependency parsing and structured training, while distinguishing equality of optimal values from identity of returned trees and training trajectories.

title: MarkovTS: Pretrained State-Transition Representations for Zero-Shot Time Series Generation
shortTitle: MarkovTS: Pretrained State-Transition Representations for Zero-Shot Time Series Generation
abstract: Across heterogeneous real-world domains, time-series generation supports simulation, model development, and data augmentation by generating sequences that preserve target-domain statistics and temporal dependencies when real observations are scarce or costly. However, existing methods predominantly address in-domain generation, limiting their reuse in unseen domains. We study reference-conditioned zero-shot time series generation: target domains are unseen during pretraining, generation uses a single target-domain reference sequence, and no model parameters are updated. MarkovTS characterizes sequence evolution through local morphologies and their ordered transitions at multiple temporal scales. Its pretrained encoder quantizes normalized time-series patches into multiscale morphological states with a state codebook, while a transition codebook encodes contextual transitions between adjacent intervals. These transferable state-transition representations condition a pretrained flow-matching model. At generation, the frozen model combines a reference-derived condition with independent Gaussian noise to produce stochastic samples that retain the reference's temporal organization. Across 12 unseen target datasets, MarkovTS outperforms strong baselines in most distributional comparisons and generates diverse, reference-consistent sequences. As downstream augmentation, its samples yield overall gains across forecasting, classification, and anomaly detection benchmarks and diverse model families. Our code is available at https://github.com/blisky-li/MarkovTS.

title: SNAPPerf: Software-Aware Tabular Foundation Model for Retraining-Free Performance Prediction of Configurable Systems
shortTitle: SNAPPerf: Software-Aware Tabular Foundation Model for Retraining-Free Performance Prediction of Configurable Systems
abstract: Modern software systems expose hundreds of configuration options whose combinations can substantially affect execution time, memory and energy usage. Measuring software performance resulting from a configuration set requires running a realistic workload. Since the configuration space grows exponentially, exhaustive benchmarking is infeasible. Prior work therefore trains models on a small set of measured configurations to predict the performance of the rest. Yet these models are specific to a particular software version, hardware platform, and workload, so changes require new measurements and retraining, and such changes are becoming more frequent with coding agents. We challenge this per-system training assumption with SNAPPERF (Software-aware, No-retraining, Adaptive Prediction), a sample-efficient tabular foundation model specialized for configurable software. SNAPPERF is pretrained once on synthetic data. Each new update only requires a few measured configurations as context to predict the rest without any per-system training or hyperparameter tuning. Across 39,866 configurations from 12 real-world systems, spanning 6 domains and 4 performance metrics, SNAPPERF reduces prediction error by 38% over the prior state of the art at the same measurement budget, and by 25% over the best general-purpose tabular foundation model. It matches the state of the art's accuracy with 54% fewer measurements on average. These results suggest that knowledge about software can be encoded in pretraining data rather than in per-system models, opening a new research direction in software-aware pretraining.

title: HieraNTP: Structured Risk Representations for Time-Series Anomaly Detection via Hierarchical Next-Token Prediction
shortTitle: HieraNTP: Structured Risk Representations for Time-Series Anomaly Detection via Hierarchical Next-Token Prediction
abstract: Time-series anomaly detection commonly converts deviations from learned temporal regularities into anomaly scores. This practice can conflate violations of temporal regularity with task-specific anomaly judgments: the same deviation may be anomalous under one task definition and benign under another. Aggregating heterogeneous deviations into a single score before task-specific adaptation can obscure the evidence needed to distinguish these cases. We introduce HieraNTP, a Hierarchical Next-Token Prediction framework that separates self-supervised predictive modeling from task-specific risk interpretation. HieraNTP pretrains a hierarchical tokenizer and a causal next-token predictor to capture temporal regularities at multiple scales. It then organizes prediction discrepancies into a structured risk representation, preserving complementary evidence across temporal scales in token, local-statistic, and observation spaces. A task-adaptive detector uses anomaly labels to select and combine this evidence for the target task. Across anomaly detection benchmarks, HieraNTP improves VUS-PR by 12.0% on TSB-AD-U and 15.5% on TSB-AD-M relative to the strongest baselines, and achieves the highest composite score on both TAB tracks, with controlled comparisons supporting the value of retaining distinct evidence. Our code is available at https://github.com/blisky-li/HieraNTP.

title: Bootstrap Inference for Riemannian Optimization Problems
shortTitle: Bootstrap Inference for Riemannian Optimization Problems
abstract: We develop an online multiplier bootstrap for manifold-valued parameters estimated by averaging the iterates of Riemannian stochastic approximation. The method runs weighted iterations alongside the original algorithm, with each path using the same observations while updating its own state and intrinsic average. The weighted averages provide uncertainty assessments without a plug-in asymptotic covariance estimator. Under local stability and regularity conditions, we establish bootstrap consistency and show that a fixed number of paths suffices for asymptotically valid Student intervals and intrinsic confidence regions. The theory accommodates samplewise nonsmooth scores and identifies a critical oracle-bias regime in which the estimator's limiting distribution shifts, but the centered bootstrap distribution does not. Applications include spherical means, positive-definite matrix means and medians, and principal-subspace estimation. Simulations show coverage close to nominal in regular settings, and an analysis of North Atlantic storm locations illustrates descriptive online inference for a spherical center.

title: Riemannian Newton Methods with Statistical Inference
shortTitle: Riemannian Newton Methods with Statistical Inference
abstract: We develop online statistical inference for Polyak-Ruppert averages of inexact Newton iterates on Riemannian manifolds. A local asymptotic representation separates observation noise, solver randomization, and accumulated implementation bias, and yields one-pass covariance estimators and asymptotically valid Wald regions under local regularity and centering conditions. Independent fresh solves add a positive semidefinite term to the score-sandwich covariance; averaging solver replicas reduces this term in inverse proportion to their number. Slowly varying predictable gains instead cancel from the first order law. Product torus simulations show how Newton scaling shortens an ill-conditioned transient and how retaining solver variation restores coverage. Intrinsic means and principal subspaces provide geometric applications, with a streaming data illustration.

title: Why Koopman Structure Does Not Help Differentiable World Models for Humanoid Whole-Body Tracking
shortTitle: Why Koopman Structure Does Not Help Differentiable World Models for Humanoid Whole-Body Tracking
abstract: We test whether Koopman structure helps a differentiable world model used to train a simulated Unitree G1 whole-body tracking policy by backpropagation through imagined rollouts, replacing the MLP world model of an otherwise unchanged pipeline. It does not: return is at best equal (0.823 versus 0.830), one-step error on identical data is 1.3 to 1.6 times the MLP's, and training is about 15% slower. Lifted rollouts diverge or fail to train policies; of the schemes tested, re-lifting at every imagined step trains best. Re-lifting never uses the lifted linear dynamics and leaves a model affine in the action, with state-dependent offset and slope; an action-affine MLP also predicts worse, so the accuracy cost belongs to this class. At a fixed state, the dynamics' curvature in the action explains only part of it. Across states, the policy's actions span a curved region, so an affine model fits policy data only as the tangent at the policy's action, the operating point: on G1, the MLP's tangent there is as accurate as the MLP; at the mean action, 31 times worse. The offset must encode, from the state alone, where the policy acts, whereas an MLP reads the action. Supplying the policy's action removes most of the remaining gap on G1, Ant and Humanoid. The only tested online repair approaching the MLP feeds the action into the nonlinear lift, abandoning the structure. For this use, the MLP world model remains the better choice.

title: PSF-Informed Reconstruction: An Enhanced 2D Directional Filtered Backprojection Method for Cone-Beam Rotary Computed Laminography
shortTitle: PSF-Informed Reconstruction: An Enhanced 2D Directional Filtered Backprojection Method for Cone-Beam Rotary Computed Laminography
abstract: Cone-beam rotary computed laminography (CL) presents a viable alternative to cone-beam CT for imaging objects with high aspect ratios. Conventional reconstruction techniques, such as CL-FBP and CL-FDK, often yield suboptimal results charac?terized by pronounced superimposition artifacts, reduced contrast,and blurred edges, primarily due to their reliance on 1D row-wise filtering along detector rows. To address these limitations and improve reconstruction quality, we proposed a novel 2D directional filtered backprojection (DFBP) method based on the point spread function (PSF). First, an exact expression for the projection process is derived by establishing the relationship between a reconstructed pixel and its corresponding projection point on the detector. Second, a revised backprojection process incorporating two weighting factors is introduced to counteract the nonlinearity inherent in conventional backprojection, leading to a simplified PSF formulation. Third, to circumvent the computational burden of 3D image space filtering,an approximate method by linearizing the coordinate relationship in Fourier space under some assumptions is developed that transfers the 3D filtering operation to the 2D projection space. This approach facilitates the derivation of a formally simple yet effective 2D direc?tional filter, which integrates a 2D von Hann window and a 2D sinc window. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method produces reconstructions with superior contrast, sharper boundaries,and fewer superimposition artifacts compared to CL-FBP and CL?FDK. Moreover, it enables more accurate recovery of internal structures, such as bubble defects and electronic components.

title: Task-Specialized Language-Conditioned Models for Fine-Grained Robotic Manipulation
shortTitle: Task-Specialized Language-Conditioned Models for Fine-Grained Robotic Manipulation

title: Evaluating Tactile Foundation Models for End-to-End Imitation Learning in Contact-Rich Manipulation

title: Self-Refining Prompt Induction for Streaming Text-to-SQL

title: 4K Image Super-Resolution on Mobile NPUs: Mobile AI 2026 Challenge Report
shortTitle: 4K Image Super-Resolution on Mobile NPUs: Mobile AI 2026 Challenge Report
abstract: Image super-resolution is widely used on mobile devices for upscaling various types of image data. In the second track, the participants were developing floating-point solutions that were evaluated on the MediaTek Dimensity 9500 NPU. title: RTP-LLM: Building an Evolvable and Reliable LLM Inference Engine at Alibaba Scale
shortTitle: RTP-LLM: Building an Evolvable and Reliable LLM Inference Engine at Alibaba Scale
abstract: Large language models and inference techniques evolve rapidly, making model enablement a recurring production task rather than a one-time integration effort. At Alibaba, a shared inference infrastructure must keep pace with new models and serving capabilities while remaining reliable across heterogeneous production environments. Its architecture separates model-specific execution from shared request processing, state management, and resource coordination. Explicit interfaces localize compatible model changes while allowing models and deployment configurations to reuse common serving mechanisms. RTP-LLM has evolved from an exploratory system into a shared production engine that supports $\sim$100 models and processes hundreds of trillions of tokens per day. We describe how its architecture and production practices accommodate model evolution and contain the impact of failures, and share lessons for building evolvable and reliable inference engines at enterprise scale.

title: Autotuning GPU Thread Block Sizes for Large-Scale Stencil Applications Using the OPS DSL
shortTitle: Autotuning GPU Thread Block Sizes for Large-Scale Stencil Applications Using the OPS DSL
abstract: Large-scale structured-mesh stencil applications can run for hours or days on modern HPC GPU platforms, making launch-configuration choices important. OPS enables high-level stencil codes to target multiple GPU architectures, but its GPU backends rely on a default or user-selected global block/workgroup shape, even though different kernels, problem geometries, and architectures may favor different configurations. This paper presents a transparent per-kernel block/workgroup-shape autotuning extension for OPS. The extension explores valid block/workgroup shapes during execution, records the fastest configuration for each kernel, and enables precomputed replay of the selected configurations in subsequent runs. We evaluate the approach on structured-mesh proxy and academic research applications, covering 459 unique kernels across 3 NVIDIA and 2 AMD GPUs. The evaluation reports speedup distributions, representative wall-time summaries, timing variability, and input problem shape effects. Replaying the best per-kernel launch shapes improves 923 of 995 measured application/input/GPU cases over the default OPS shape. Depending on the GPU, the median speedup ranges from 1.02x to 1.18x, with individual configurations of LAPL2D, TTI3D, and OpenSBLI-based TGV solvers exceeding 1.5x. The results also show that performance sensitivity is not limited to launch shape. At fixed cell count, changing the input problem shape changes precomputed-replay runtime by 0.8-34.6% in representative cases, while kernel-level timing variability depends on the interaction between runtime contribution, input problem shape, and GPU/backend behavior. Overall, automatic per-kernel block/workgroup-shape selection improves OPS performance across GPUs, provided shape sensitivity and timing stability are interpreted together.

title: Efficient Image Denoising on Smartphone GPUs: Mobile AI 2026 Challenge Report
shortTitle: Efficient Image Denoising on Smartphone GPUs: Mobile AI 2026 Challenge Report
abstract: Image denoising is a fundamental problem in mobile photography. Despite a large number of solutions proposed for this task, the majority of them are trained on synthetically produced noisy images, and are additionally too computationally heavy for processing full-resolution images on mobile devices. This creates a need for efficient deep learning-based models that are not only performant but can also be deployed on constrained mobile hardware. In this Mobile AI challenge, we address this problem and propose the participants to design fast solutions that can denoise Full HD resolution photos while running on popular smartphone GPUs from Qualcomm and Arm. For this, the participants were provided with a large-scale dataset consisting of noisy-clean image pairs captured in the wild. The runtime of all models was evaluated on the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and Dimensity 9500 chipsets with the Adreno and Mali GPUs, respectively. Top solutions proposed in this challenge are able to perform high-quality image denoising under 100 milliseconds on both platforms while reaching a PSNR score of over 37 dB. A comprehensive description of the models developed in the challenge is provided in this paper.

title: A Token Is Not a Unit of Difficulty: Segmentation Controls Where Adaptive Computation Goes Inside a Word
shortTitle: A Token Is Not a Unit of Difficulty: Segmentation Controls Where Adaptive Computation Goes Inside a Word
abstract: Early-exit language models decide for each token how much computation to spend, usually by stopping once the prediction is confident. Yet a token is not a fixed unit: tokenizers cut words into different numbers of pieces in different languages. We ask where inside a word such a policy spends its budget. In Qwen3, along two adaptive axes (the timesteps of a spiking conversion and the layers of the original Transformer), confidence stopping gives the continuation pieces of a word less computation than its first piece in English, German, and Turkish, but more in Bangla. Segmentation drives this. Re-segmenting the same parallel passages with BPE-dropout shifts the gap by up to eight exits on both axes, small models trained under two tokenizers shift Bangla's gap by six exits, and BLOOM and mGPT, which split Bangla less finely, give it the English pattern. Characters per token do not predict the gap across languages; within-word surprisal explains 75% of its variance. A learned stopping head beats confidence stopping by 7 to 8 points, but gains less than one point over the best mix of fixed exits at equal cost, and sometimes loses. All results come from offline analysis, not measured speedups.

title: HALO: Hierarchical Evidence Selection and Reinforcement Learning for Allocating Budgeted Label Optimization from Longitudinal Clinical Records
shortTitle: HALO: Hierarchical Evidence Selection and Reinforcement Learning for Allocating Budgeted Label Optimization from Longitudinal Clinical Records
abstract: Learning from extensive longitudinal clinical records--spanning repeated encounters, evolving conditions, and heterogeneous documentation--under a finite labeling budget requires solving two coupled problems: deciding what evidence to keep and deciding which patients deserve higher-fidelity labels. Prior work on active learning and multi-fidelity label acquisition mainly addresses the second problem, while treating the evidence presented to the acquisition policy as fixed. We present HALO, a Hierarchical Evidence Selection and Reinforcement Learning pipeline for Allocating Budgeted Label Optimization from Longitudinal Clinical Records. This framework jointly learns what to read and what label source to acquire under budget. HALO first selects informative evidence from longitudinal records and then uses a budget-aware policy to allocate free-, silver-, and gold-fidelity label sources. For frozen policies, our theory characterizes asymmetric acquired-label channels and gives a budget-constrained finite-sample gold-risk bound for a common downstream logistic model. In a heart-failure case study, HALO attained the highest MedAlign acquired-label F1 at six of eight target budgets. A downstream classifier trained on HALO-acquired labels attained the highest external MGB F1 at budgets 15-60 and remained within 0.01 of the best comparator at budgets 75-120.

title: Pulse: Long-Horizon Tasks Need Streaming Personalization
shortTitle: Pulse: Long-Horizon Tasks Need Streaming Personalization
abstract: Large language model agents increasingly undertake complex, long-horizon tasks that benefit from sustained personalized support through long-term memory. Existing memory-augmented methods retrieve and use memory primarily from the initial request, with limited awareness of ongoing execution and emerging personalization needs. Agents may therefore overlook user preferences and project constraints during multistep tasks. We propose Pulse, a streaming personalization method for long-horizon tasks. An independent, lightweight memory agent continuously monitors execution, identifies emerging personalization needs and potential preference conflicts, and uses user and project memories to provide targeted interventions at appropriate stages. Reinforcement learning optimizes when and how the memory agent intervenes, improving the timeliness and accuracy of personalized support. Pulse scores 71.9% on $π$-Bench and 46.4% on MCP-Persona, achieving the highest overall scores among the compared methods on both datasets while improving task execution efficiency.

title: GURU: A Hierarchical Neuro-Symbolic Multi-Agent System for Verification-Aware Automation of Mission-Critical Digital Engineering and Operations
shortTitle: GURU: A Hierarchical Neuro-Symbolic Multi-Agent System for Verification-Aware Automation of Mission-Critical Digital Engineering and Operations
abstract: An AI can find a safe action faster than any human, but it must never decide what counts as safe. We present GURU, a hierarchical neuro-symbolic multi-agent system for mission-critical digital engineering and operations, built on one partition of authority: learned models propose, rank, and accelerate; a symbolic rules engine checks every consequential action against hard limits before it executes; and validated physics confirms and decides. GURU runs a workflow as a closed control loop, with Navigation, Action, and Planning agents sharing one Common Internal Language and one training factory. Nuclear, aviation, and national-security guidance now requires this pattern; a harnessed language model keeps the model at the center, GURU puts a validated reference there. In computational fluid dynamics, the workflow raised the converged-simulation rate on unseen aircraft geometries from under 1 percent to 74 percent over 100 single-attempt cases, ran 54 live cases to Mach 6 on three facilities, and an ablation put the symbolic layer at 13 points of boundary-layer capture. Knowledge-graph retrieval and role adapters raised ParaView control success from 55 to 75 percent. In space domain awareness, where a language model cannot be trusted to decide, a frozen self-supervised world model under validated propagation scored highest of five methods at conjunction risk, including fully fine-tuned language models, with several-times-lower seed variance: the trustworthy design gives up nothing in accuracy, and the recipe transferred to reactor anomaly detection. A radar-to-avoidance debris pipeline was demonstrated in stages on a 2026 reentry; the hierarchy coordinates simulated teams of 200 aircraft. Training scaled near-linearly past 1,000 Aurora nodes and ran at 8,000. The approach extends to a control-grade microreactor digital twin with validated physics, not a learned model, as the safety basis.

title: Leap-VLA: High-Rate Robot Control from a Low-Rate VLM Backbone
shortTitle: Leap-VLA: High-Rate Robot Control from a Low-Rate VLM Backbone
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models re-encode the full observation through a multi-billion-parameter vision-language model (VLM) at every control step, even though scene semantics evolve at roughly 1 Hz while reactive control requires 20-50 Hz. We present a VLA that decouples the two: a VLM runs as a low-frequency semantic anchor whose cached context is reused across control steps, while a flow-matching action expert operates at high frequency, consuming the cached semantics with a fresh, low-latency visual stream from a compact encoder pretrained on robot video with masked reconstruction, optical flow, and depth. The measured age $τ$ of the cache conditions the expert through adaptive layer normalization. Reusing the cache makes the policy a function of its age, and training covers that function explicitly: cache ages sampled from real episode history, plus an age-ramped pixel corruption that erases the stale snapshot the way deployed staleness corrupts content. On the asynchronous deployment stack, the recipe closes most of the staleness gap: on LIBERO-Spatial, 61.4% to 95.5% at a 2 s semantic refresh (95.9% at 1 s, within 1.6 points of the frequency-matched anchor); averaged over the four LIBERO suites, the deployed policy holds 95.2% at a 1 s refresh and 94.5% at 2 s against a 96.3% matched anchor. A forward-only chunk-boundary correction (soft-nudge), an autograd-free reformulation of real-time-chunking guidance, carries per-control-step re-planning without loss (97.1%) at zero added latency. The same lens exposes a second defect: under an instruction-scene mismatch the policy keeps manipulating the scene, and a chain-of-thought verdict gate trained on zero-cost negative episodes freezes execution exactly on mismatched instructions without hurting feasible success.

title: IJev: Order-Invariant Decisions via Iterated Cyclic Reordering
shortTitle: IJev: Order-Invariant Decisions via Iterated Cyclic Reordering
abstract: System One decision models answer a choice question in one forward pass, but their answer depends on the order in which options are listed, and their probabilities carry a prior over answer labels. An invariant ordering operator is any fixed function that returns the same ordered option list for every input order of a fixed option set. Starting from any such order and averaging a listwise readout over its K cyclic shifts removes the input order, but the decision still depends on the chosen cyclic class: those $K$ shifts are only one of the (K-1)! classes, and different invariant operators can select different classes. We propose IJev, which repeatedly reorders the options by the cyclic-averaged, label-prior-corrected distribution and runs another cyclic average. Every iterate is exactly input-order-invariant. When the iteration does not converge, we average the round distributions rather than return the last round. On five benchmarks and five models, IJev has flip rate zero in every cell. The default uniform average over T=20 rounds substantially improves calibration over a single cyclic average, and its accuracy is comparable. A descriptive choice of horizon and averaging rule is best or tied-best for accuracy in all 25 settings.

title: Robust Pixel-wise Digital Image Correlation under Large Motions and Illumination Variations via a Global-to-Local Hybrid Neural Field
shortTitle: Robust Pixel-wise Digital Image Correlation under Large Motions and Illumination Variations via a Global-to-Local Hybrid Neural Field
abstract: Digital image correlation (DIC) is a widely used non-contact technique for full-field displacement measurement. Data-driven deep-learning DIC offers rapid inference but may generalize poorly to unseen speckle patterns, deformation modes, noise levels, and illumination conditions. Classical optimization-based DIC and recent image-constrained neural formulations avoid labeled displacement data, yet their convergence and accuracy remain vulnerable to initialization, large rigid-body motion, fine non-uniform deformation, and gray-value disturbances. This paper presents a global-to-local hybrid neural DIC framework for robust pixelwise measurement. Stage 1 estimates a dominant in-plane rigid transformation through coarse rotation search, phase correlation, and masked refinement, providing a reliable initialization under large translation and rotation. Stage 2 represents the residual displacement with a hybrid Kolmogorov-Arnold network (KAN) and multilayer perceptron (MLP), and optimizes it using a valid-overlap, illumination-robust structural loss. The local gray-value model explicitly accommodates multiplicative and additive intensity changes. Simulated and real experiments demonstrate accurate and stable displacement recovery under noise, non-uniform deformation, large rotation, illumination variation, and degraded imaging conditions.

title: Jet-QSparse: Accelerating Agentic LLM Inference with 4-Bit Sparse Attention
shortTitle: Jet-QSparse: Accelerating Agentic LLM Inference with 4-Bit Sparse Attention
abstract: Long-horizon reasoning and agentic workloads strain KV-cache capacity and decode attention throughput. We present Jet-QSparse, a training-free method that combines compact NVFP4 cache storage with native FP4 query-key computation on Blackwell tensor cores. A dense scan scores the full key history and selects 128-token blocks for sparse FP16 value aggregation with FP32 accumulation, preserving higher precision in the output-forming step while enabling contiguous tile loads. Calibrated key centering and at most two BF16 pages per sequence and layer address quantization error; FP8 prefill uses a temporary arena while the persistent cache is packed directly from BF16 activations. Across four hybrid LLMs, a budget of 128 blocks per KV head shows no detected accuracy loss on the evaluated mathematical reasoning, coding, and agentic benchmarks, although some smaller budgets incur losses. With 64 blocks, Qwen3.8-27B achieves a $1.94\times$ end-to-end decode speedup over dense BF16 at 128K context and batch size 16 on one GB300, and the measured Qwen KV pools provide $2.58$-$2.76\times$ BF16's token capacity.

title: Hierarchical Asynchronous Federated Learning over Space-Air-Ground Integrated Networks
shortTitle: Hierarchical Asynchronous Federated Learning over Space-Air-Ground Integrated Networks
abstract: With the emerging 6G paradigm where AI services operate over decentralized and resource-constrained edge infrastructure, performance of distributed learning algorithms remains a significant challenge. This paper proposes HAFL, a Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite-assisted hierarchical asynchronous Federated Learning (FL) framework, enabling resource-limited terrestrial clients to collaborate via Ground-Satellite Links (GSLs). Within this framework, LEO satellites serve multiple roles: as edge servers aggregating and broadcasting models, as clients accelerating training, and as high-throughput relays managing inter-satellite routing through Inter-Satellite Links (ISLs). title: Forecasting Visitor Demand from Open AI-Camera Counts and Weather: Lessons from Japan for Saudi Heritage Sites
shortTitle: Forecasting Visitor Demand from Open AI-Camera Counts and Weather: Lessons from Japan for Saudi Heritage Sites
abstract: Small heritage and nature sites need a few days' notice of busy days to plan staff, overflow parking and shuttles, but most have neither sensors nor forecasting expertise. We test what one artificial intelligence (AI) camera counter per site, a public holiday calendar and a free weather forecast can predict. Using 22 months of open AI-camera counts from three contrasting sites in Fukui, Japan (a train station, a coastal cliff and a mountain summit park), we measure how weather changes visits, forecast daily counts up to a week ahead with only the weather forecast available at the time, test busy-day warnings tied to a staffing decision, and ask how much history a new counter needs. The more exposed the site, the more weather matters: 10 mm of rain comes with 3% fewer detections at the station, 9% fewer at the cliff and 37% fewer at the summit park. With the forecasts actually issued, three-day-ahead weighted absolute percentage error (WAPE) at the summit park falls from 38.5% to 31.9% (Diebold-Mariano p<0.001), and the gain holds to five days; the sheltered station gains nothing. Three-day busy-day warnings with forecast weather reach, on past data and under the primary definitions, an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.87-0.93, and weather lifts the overflow car park warning's precision from 0.60 to 0.82. For a new counter, blending a learned model with last week's same-hour counts cuts hourly error after only three days of training, pending a real installation. All inputs are off the shelf, and we outline how the approach could apply to heritage sites in Saudi Arabia.

title: Self-Normalized Inference from Riemannian Stochastic Gradient Paths
shortTitle: Self-Normalized Inference from Riemannian Stochastic Gradient Paths
abstract: Riemannian stochastic gradient paths estimate constrained parameters, but confidence regions usually require estimating the Hessian and gradient-noise covariance. We develop self-normalized inference from one path by expressing retained iterates in a common random tangent space. Their average and centered partial sums share an unknown covariance factor that cancels in a Brownian bridge pivot. Under suitable regularity conditions, a joint expansion of the averaged estimator and integrated path controls nonlinear coordinate errors using conditional second moments. The procedure uses fixed-dimensional memory and extends to nondegenerate smooth functionals and alternative local coordinates. Numerical studies show competitive coverage relative to plug-in Wald inference while avoiding Hessian and residual-density estimation.

title: HALO-LP: A Homogeneous All-Shifted Non-Interior-Point Method for Linear Programming
shortTitle: HALO-LP: A Homogeneous All-Shifted Non-Interior-Point Method for Linear Programming
abstract: This letter introduces HALO-LP, a novel homogeneous all-shifted non-interior-point method for linear programming (LP). The proposed method combines a homogeneous self-dual (HSD) embedding with all-shifted nonlinear complementarity (NCP) functions and proximal primal-dual regularization, enabling arbitrary primal-dual warm starts without requiring strictly interior iterates. The resulting Newton equations admit a condensation based on a positive-definite matrix that can be efficiently factorized using Cholesky decomposition, while the HSD embedding enables primal and dual infeasibility detection through Farkas certificates. Numerical evaluations on perturbed LP instances derived from the Netlib test set demonstrate state-of-the-art warm-starting performance, outperforming the competing solvers in the evaluated setting. We further validate optimality and infeasibility detection on analytically characterized LP problems. Finally, we demonstrate HALO-LP's applicability to robotic optimal control through sequential linear programming (SLP) for centroidal walking and trotting of quadrupedal robots.

title: pico-WAM: Evaluating Counterfactual Prediction and Planning Error in a Compact World Action Model

These controlled interventions identify scoring as an effective improvement target in the tested setting and provide a reproducible protocol for diagnosing compact world models.

title: Constraint Dependency Graph Retrieval for Compliance Detection on Long SKILL Documents
shortTitle: Constraint Dependency Graph Retrieval for Compliance Detection on Long SKILL Documents
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents carry out business operations under enterprise documents we refer to as SKILL documents, which take the form of standard operating procedures (SOPs) that state the conditions to verify and the actions to take before an operation proceeds. Long, densely cross-referenced SKILL documents exceed the context budget of small deployed auditors. Similarity-based retrieval then brings in irrelevant rules while omitting mandatory prerequisites, and the two-stage audit policy provides no trainable signal for the retrieval stage. We present SkillCDG, a compliance detection framework that reformulates each SKILL document as a constraint dependency graph, shifting rule retrieval from similarity-based matching to closure-based selection under the deployment's context budget. Each atomic rule is anchored to its source text span as a graph node, and mandatory prerequisite relations form the sole edge type. Policy-generated retrieval keywords activate seed rules, whose dependency closure yields a compact and conditionally complete rule context within that budget. The same graph also supports a joint optimization scheme. The retrieval stage is trained with group-relative policy optimization using a verifiable reward that combines output-format validity with downstream verdict correctness, with closure non-emptiness serving as a validity gate, while selective on-policy distillation concentrates teacher supervision on high-entropy reasoning tokens, with verdict and termination tokens always included, to improve verdict accuracy. Experiments on three enterprise datasets and two public benchmarks show that SkillCDG improves accuracy and F1 over the full-document and retrieval-based baselines.

title: Dependable Agents Need Hard and Fuzzy Rules
shortTitle: Dependable Agents Need Hard and Fuzzy Rules
abstract: Language models let software read requests in ordinary language, but they keep rules as people do: usually, and less so under pressure. Conventional code keeps rules exactly, but it cannot read a request. We argue that dependable agents need both, because the two kinds of rule cover overlapping and unequal regions of what an agent might do. Code holds the limits that can be stated exactly. Learned fuzzy rules cover the judgment that cannot. We test the hard layer in three domains, purchasing, delegation of authority and data access, on 1,340 episodes written by authors outside our team. Models left to decide for themselves executed unauthorized actions in up to 151 of 340 purchasing episodes and 269 of 470 delegation episodes, and the strongest model breached in every condition. A hard guard between proposal and action executed none, and an exhaustive search of 183,204 proposals agreed. In a further test, where an outsider wrote the owner's rules and a program mapped them to the guard, two episodes breached at a boundary we had written down in advance. We then test the pair. Concept Programming instills a named rule in a model and measures its errors on wording it never saw. A small model taught four judgment rules this way flagged 95 of 96 rule-breaking purchases that no exact rule can see, and 4 of 108 legitimate requests. Placed in front of the guard, it left 1 of 192 rule-breaking requests unstopped, where the guard alone left 77 and 70, and the guard still held every exact limit. title: Investigating ET-SoC-1 Vector and Parallel Performance with sGEMM
shortTitle: Investigating ET-SoC-1 Vector and Parallel Performance with sGEMM
abstract: The Ainekko (formerly Esperanto) ET-SoC-1 is a massively parallel RISC-V accelerator. Two device kernels are implemented and evaluated on the ET-SoC-1, these are a register-blocked PS SIMD baseline with two-step software pipelining, and a TensorFMA32 kernel that drives the same FMA datapath through the per-core tensor micro-operation sequencer, with double-buffered A scratchpad loading. Because both kernels are bounded by the same arithmetic peak, the comparison isolates the effect of operand delivery from that of arithmetic width. Performance is compared against CPU references (SpacemiT K3, Intel i5-11600, AMD Ryzen 9 9950X and the Arm Cortex-X925/A725 CPU of an NVIDIA DGX Spark) and two GPUs (NVIDIA GB10 Blackwell and AMD RDNA4 RX 9060 XT).

title: Entropy-Regularized Reinforcement Learning for the Regime-Switching Consumption-Investment Problem
shortTitle: Entropy-Regularized Reinforcement Learning for the Regime-Switching Consumption-Investment Problem
abstract: This paper establishes an entropy-regularized reinforcement learning (ERRL) framework for the continuous-time consumption-investment problem under a regime-switching market model with general utility functions. By incorporating randomized exploratory policies and Shannon entropy regularization into the stochastic optimal control formulation, we derive closed-form representations for the optimal exploratory consumption and investment strategies. Specifically, the optimal investment strategy follows a multivariate Gaussian distribution, whereas the optimal consumption strategy takes the form of a Gibbs measure---which specializes to a Gamma distribution under logarithmic utility and a non-standard exponential distribution under power utility. Crucially, our theoretical analysis reveals that the classical deterministic optimal decisions correspond to the mode---rather than the mean---of these exploratory distributions. Furthermore, we establish the convergence of the exploratory value function to its classical unregularized counterpart as the temperature parameter vanishes. For algorithmic design, we develop a continuous-time q-learning framework grounded in a novel continuous-time q-function, prove the policy improvement theorem, and establish martingale characterizations for both on-policy and off-policy learning. We find that parameterizing the actor network based on theoretical distribution families can help accelerate convergence and enhance numerical stability. Furthermore, numerical experiments across regime-switching environments provide empirical support for our theoretical findings, demonstrating stable loss convergence as well as the monotonicity and concavity of the learned value functions.

title: Infinite Worlds from One Example: What Local Generators Must Share
shortTitle: Infinite Worlds from One Example: What Local Generators Must Share
abstract: Seeded noise lets games generate any region of an unbounded world on demand. We ask what such a generator needs when every small window must come from one example, the constraint behind Wave Function Collapse. The difficulty is that local constraints can require agreement over arbitrary distances: in a brick wall, each row keeps its place between the mortar lines. We study local generators, each cell a fixed function of the randomness near it. When the constraints carry a quantity that varies across the example, no generator that applies one rule, ignoring position, to independent randomness at every cell can be both exactly valid and faithful to the example's statistics, however far each cell reads. At radius r, staying faithful forces forbidden windows at a density of at least order 1/r, and a construction attains this order. To vary the quantity between exactly valid worlds, a generator needs randomness shared along its direction. We give a finitely checkable condition under which row types drawn from the seed and the position modulo a fixed period suffice for exact validity without learning. A search over the example's patches certifies these quantities and names the input each needs. Across 52 public examples of Wave Function Collapse and 27 from other implementations, it certifies only examples where a learned generator on independent randomness stays far from valid after repair. Given that input, a neural cellular automaton and a diffusion model become valid on 10 and 8 of the 12 certified examples that receive one, and on none from independent randomness. Valid means at most one forbidden window in a thousand after repair. With octaves of seeded noise elsewhere, the automaton is valid on 45 of the 52 public examples and 21 of the 27 from other implementations, and repair keeps random access.

title: Adaptive Land Units from Earth Embeddings
shortTitle: Adaptive Land Units from Earth Embeddings
abstract: Modeling land use starts with a choice of spatial units, typically a regular grid of pixels whose resolution is set by the spatial detail the process requires and, often more critically, by the computational budget. With Earth observation data more abundant than ever, we ask whether good land units can instead emerge from the data itself. To do that, we cluster AlphaEarth embeddings with a parallel Bayesian hierarchical clustering into adaptive land units, large where the land is uniform and small where it is highly heterogeneous. Using Denmark as a case study, we turn 402M land pixels into 1.27M newly defined units, about 320 times fewer, without any labels (i.e., unsupervised), making it possible to fit the whole country on a single consumer-grade GPU. Importantly, these units describe the land well, as a regular grid needs about 5 times as many cells to match them against land-use labels, and about 4 times as many against the declared crop of every field. Compared to clustering the satellite images themselves, the embeddings need half the units for the same purity. But more notably, they work as modeling units. Land-use maps learned on them are within a few points of accuracy of pixel models at a small fraction of the cost, and they make whole-country land-use estimates with reliable uncertainty possible in under a minute, where the same model on pixels does not even fit in device memory.

title: Temperature, Not Knowledge: What Recursive Self-Training and Its Remedies Do to a Language Model's Confidence
shortTitle: Temperature, Not Knowledge: What Recursive Self-Training and Its Remedies Do to a Language Model's Confidence
abstract: Recursive self-training can collapse language models, and many proposed remedies target overconfidence, yet their effects on confidence are rarely measured. We study a five-round self-training loop on Qwen3-1.7B, using three seeds per compared method, and distinguish confidence temperature (drift from a calibrated starting point) from discrimination (ranking correct answers above incorrect ones). Accuracy and overall discrimination remain nearly unchanged, but confidence sharpens and the most confident answers become less reliable. Matching predictive entropy to the calibrated starting model each round recalibrates nearly as well as label-based temperature fitting, at both 1.7B and 8B. Sharpening is not inherent to self-training: exact samples from a model's distribution have zero expected gradient. Instead, most drift comes from fitting each generated answer twice, with top-p truncation contributing the rest; removing both keeps entropy on generated outputs flat. Remedies affect the two properties differently: truncated cross-entropy, an entropy bonus, and single-pass training preserve temperature without improving discrimination, while focal loss and multi-sample targets improve discrimination but cause underconfidence. Reference-data mixing also overshoots. Pairing a ranking-improving loss with label-free recalibration achieves both.

title: Robust Reward Machine Learning and Execution in Noisy Environments
shortTitle: Robust Reward Machine Learning and Execution in Noisy Environments
abstract: Background: Reward machines (RMs) represent non-Markovian reward functions as finite-state machines over high-level propositional events. Traditionally, these events are generated by a deterministic labelling function that maps environment states to proposition sets. However, real-world labelling functions are inherently noisy. Objectives: Design and implement a method that learns RMs in the presence of noisy labelling functions and exploits them for policy learning in both discrete and continuous environments. Methods: We propose Prob-IRM, a method that learns RMs from noisy proposition histories using inductive logic programming (ILP) and exploits them for policy learning. Noisy proposition histories are represented as training examples for ILP, which learns an RM that maximises coverage of low-uncertainty histories. RM learning is interleaved with policy optimisation. Prob-IRM uses a belief over RM states to determine when to relearn the RM and to provide additional guiding rewards. Results: Prob-IRM is evaluated on environments with discrete and continuous state spaces under varying levels of labelling noise. Prob-IRM performs comparably to baselines using handcrafted RMs and outperforms approaches that use recurrent neural networks to encode history, despite operating with noisy labels. Conclusions: Prob-IRM represents a step towards deploying reward machines in noisy, real-world environments.

title: Label Smoothing in Disguise? Gated Knowledge Distillation for Low-Resource Bangla Generation
shortTitle: Label Smoothing in Disguise? Gated Knowledge Distillation for Low-Resource Bangla Generation
abstract: Gated knowledge distillation (KD) weights teacher signals per token or example, aiming to trust an imperfect teacher only where it seems reliable. We test two gates: EWAD (entropy-weighted agreement-aware distillation), which gates tokens by teacher confidence, and CHAD (counterfactual harm-aware distillation), which gates examples by gradient alignment with validation data. Across six Bangla-centric tasks, three student models (60M to about 2B parameters), and two teacher families, no gate significantly improves plain KD in 45 comparisons. KD also fails to beat cross-entropy (CE) fine-tuning on gold outputs in 40 single-seed comparisons or three-seed runs on four tasks; CE leads on every summarisation metric. The main benefit of KD is regularisation: over ten fixed epochs, CE students lose 0.030 to 0.044 token-F1 from their early-stopped checkpoint, versus 0.005 to 0.025 for distilled students. Teacher-free label smoothing closes most of this gap. In one comparison, a teacher 0.29 token-F1 worse yields students at most 0.009 worse. Thus, gating may change regularisation strength but has little teacher knowledge to select. Findings are limited to Bangla-centric tasks and small students. We will release code, data splits, predictions, and scores.

title: Ripple: Deadline-Aware CPU-GPU Sharing for Embodied Inference
shortTitle: Ripple: Deadline-Aware CPU-GPU Sharing for Embodied Inference
abstract: Unified-memory edge devices increasingly run LLM/VLM inference alongside time-critical CPU tasks for perception and control. GPU memory traffic can overwhelm these tasks, yet platforms such as DGX Spark expose neither bandwidth counters nor direct bandwidth regulation. We present Ripple, a CPU-GPU co-scheduler that combines model-derived GPU memory volumes with CPU completion feedback to regulate interference. Ripple divides inference into pausable, layer-based units and translates each CPU job's deadline slack into a GPU-byte budget, admitting work within the budgets of all overlapping jobs. Online updates track changing interference, while deadline-aware pacing and judicious SM footprint narrowing preserve inference progress. Implemented with SGLang engine hooks and a central scheduler, we evaluate Ripple on DGX Spark with four robotic CPU task mixes and LLM/VLM inference. It is the only evaluated approach that consistently meets the 2% CPU deadline-miss target and VLM deadlines across the tested deadline settings while retaining best-effort LLM throughput.

title: On Sparse Graph Limits for Neural Combinatorial Optimization
shortTitle: On Sparse Graph Limits for Neural Combinatorial Optimization
abstract: Graph neural networks are often trained on small graphs and deployed on larger ones, raising the question of which graph information must be preserved for combinatorial optimization values to transfer across sizes. We establish size-transfer guarantees for normalized graph optimization values using finite collections of energy features. For affine objectives, including MAX-CUT, coloring defect, and independent-set density, differences in task value are controlled by discrepancies in normalized scalar energy probes on all bounded-degree graphs. For general Lipschitz objectives, such as those with balance penalties, an additional representation error appears; this error vanishes on hyperfinite graph families but can remain bounded away from zero on expanders. Thus, at fixed degree bound, state space, Lipschitz constant, and target accuracy, a finite energy representation independent of graph size suffices universally for affine tasks and asymptotically for general Lipschitz tasks on hyperfinite families. These results yield prediction guarantees under explicit conditions on encoder accuracy, readout stability, and representation coverage, together with statistical generalization bounds. Theoretically, we prove Shapley-Folkman bounds with sharp parameter dependence, including a dimension-free $\ell_2$ regime, and realize the resulting energy features with a fixed-weight message-passing network using random node initialization on bounded-treewidth graphs. Experiments with exact solvers and trained models test the resulting transfer guarantees.

title: Hi-CoLA: High Confidence Lower Bound Approximation Based Reinforcement Learning for Flex-Route Transit Operation Control
shortTitle: Hi-CoLA: High Confidence Lower Bound Approximation Based Reinforcement Learning for Flex-Route Transit Operation Control
abstract: This paper studies safe policy improvement for real-time operation control of flex-route transit (FRT) systems, where robustness is critical and any performance decrease is undesirable. While reinforcement learning (RL) has shown strong empirical success, its adoption remains limited in safety and cost critical applications, such as intelligent transportation, since learned policies lack statistically certified performance guarantees before deployment. In this paper, we propose the High Confidence Lower Bound Approximation (Hi-CoLA) RL framework, which combines importance sampling and concentration inequalities with a differentiable surrogate network to efficiently estimate the high-confidence performance lower bound and optimize it via policy gradient for robust performance improvement. On the FRT operation control problem, Hi-CoLA outperforms state-of-the-art offline and safe RL methods in both average and tail-risk performance. A case study on an actual route in Chicago, implemented in the SUMO simulator, serves as a proof of concept. Hi-CoLA enhances real-time FRT control with guaranteed performance and is broadly applicable to other safety critical decision-making scenarios.

title: Grounding Across Views: Cross-View Referring Reasoning for Visual Grounding
shortTitle: Grounding Across Views: Cross-View Referring Reasoning for Visual Grounding
abstract: Cross-view object geo-localization (CVOGL) aims to localize a target in a satellite image from an observation captured under another viewpoint. Existing methods typically specify the query with a click point or bounding box, marking the target region but underusing the semantic attributes and relations conveyed by natural language. Moreover, referring expressions are often viewpoint-dependent, making query-view descriptions difficult to ground directly in the satellite image. In this paper, we formulate cross-view visual grounding (CVVG), extending conventional point- or box-prompted CVOGL to instance grounding jointly guided by a referring expression and a visual exemplar. We present GAV (Grounding Across Views), a view-aware framework for selectively transferring visual and linguistic evidence across views. Its core is view-aware referring reasoning: target-centered descriptions are derived from the marked query image, checked for target-category consistency, and augmented with a direction-free role cue. Exemplar prompting, cross-view alignment, and scene-level discrimination ground this semantic evidence in a satellite instance. GAV achieves a new state of the art on MoP-UAV with 62.55% Acc@0.5. We also introduce CVOGL-Text, a benchmark for text-guided grounding from street- and drone-view queries to satellite images. GAV outperforms the click-point baseline by 7.09 and 6.79 Acc@0.25 points on the street- and drone-view splits, respectively, demonstrating robustness to larger viewpoint gaps. The code and annotations will be publicly released.
