title: Multi-Turn Semantic Caching for Low-Cost LLM Serving
shortTitle: Multi-Turn Semantic Caching for Low-Cost LLM Serving
abstract: Semantic caching lowers the cost of serving large language models (LLMs) by reusing stored responses for similar requests. In multi-turn conversations, whether a cached response is acceptable depends on both conversations' histories, which embedding similarity of requests and histories predicts poorly (AUC 0.62--0.74 on five workloads). We therefore learn the \emph{reuse risk}, the probability that a cached response is unacceptable, from judge feedback, and choose a budgeted set of conversation states to cache by weighing the generation cost a reuse avoids against a price for unacceptable reuse. We propose CUCB-SC-MT, which learns a cache from logged conversations with a suboptimality guarantee, and CLCB-LS-MT, which learns online and has $\tilde O(\sqrt N)$ regret over $N$ requests when conversation states recur. On math-tutoring (SocraTeach) and movie-ticketing (Taskmaster-3) conversations, both achieve lower loss than prior semantic caching approaches: ContextCache, multi-turn variants of ElastiCache and vCache, and single-turn semantic caching at every cache budget. With 1,000 cache entries, CLCB-LS-MT avoids 35--41\% of the generation cost through acceptable reuses, against at most 22--25\% for the baselines, and lowers estimated serving latency by 19--35\%.

title: CuPH: Parallel Cubical Persistent Homology via Level-Synchronous Component Tracking
shortTitle: CuPH: Parallel Cubical Persistent Homology via Level-Synchronous Component Tracking
abstract: Persistent homology (PH) is a mathematically principled multi-scale topological descriptor of shape and connectivity in data. It is widely applied in image classification, segmentation, and shape analysis across medical and aerial imaging, providing structural information that pixel-wise deep learning may overlook. Standard cubical PH decomposes an image into cubical cells (vertices, edges, and squares) and reduces them sequentially in filtration order. This sequential reduction has $Θ(n)$ parallel depth for an $n$-pixel image, limiting within-image GPU parallelism and constraining its use in topology-aware deep learning. We introduce CuPH, a GPU-based parallel algorithm for computing cubical PH on 2D images that operates directly on pixels rather than cubical cells. CuPH buckets pixels by filtration values, activates them with a level-synchronous sweep, and tracks connected components with a lock-free union-find method. We prove that CuPH produces persistence diagrams identical to standard cubical PH on integer inputs, with a stability bound for floating-point inputs. CuPH reduces parallel depth from $Θ(n)$ to $O(L\log n)$ for an image with $L$ intensity levels. We implement the level sweep as a single CUDA kernel, eliminating cross-level kernel-launch overhead. Empirically, CuPH is $18.6$--$99.6\times$ faster than the existing GPU baseline (CMP). As a drop-in PH backend, CuPH accelerates topology-aware classification ($4.2$--$16.7\times$) and segmentation ($8.3$--$44\times$) while preserving accuracy. It also enables computing full-image PH losses on high-resolution images, improving segmentation Dice by $2.2$--$4.6$ points over patch-local PH baselines and accelerating training by $25$--$31\times$.

title: Robust Safety Assurance for Robotic Swarms Using Decentralized Collision Verification
shortTitle: Robust Safety Assurance for Robotic Swarms Using Decentralized Collision Verification
abstract: In this paper we present the methodologies, results, and analysis used to deploy a decentralized safety verification algorithm on a robotic swarm to prevent collisions at runtime in an outdoor environment. Typically, approaches toward verification of swarms of cyber-physical systems (CPS) are evaluated solely in numerical simulations or in highly controlled, noiseless indoor environments. Our efforts to implement collision avoidance on a real swarm system outdoors have revealed that the underlying algorithmic assumptions juxtaposed against the implementation details of the target system are critical factors in a method's efficacy in the real world. Here we modify, enhance, and analyze a decentralized reachability-based method for collision avoidance on a size, weight, and power-constrained uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) swarm with the objective of illustrating the challenges of real-world CPS deployments as well as provide guidance for researchers in this space. Verification performance, resource utilization, and timing data were gathered over the course of 140 total outdoor vehicle flights, including 6 swarm flights composed of 8 UAVs, and used to improve collision-avoidance performance as experimentation progressed. Our extensive experiments show that the proposed decentralized runtime verification approach can efficiently verify the safety of multiple UAVs in real-time and help all agents take safe actions to avoid collisions. On average, each agent, using our open-source safety_checker library, takes approximately 500-520 ms to verify its safety for the next 4 s into the future, in which the reachable set broadcast time dominates the total verification time (~300-500 ms).

title: QVR3D: Query-Guided Visual Reasoning for Training-Free 3D Grounding
shortTitle: QVR3D: Query-Guided Visual Reasoning for Training-Free 3D Grounding
abstract: 3D visual grounding localizes objects in 3D scenes from natural language descriptions, requiring reasoning over semantics, spatial relationships, and multi-view observations. Training-free approaches avoid costly annotations but often rely on explicit scene transformation or scene-level frame selection, which may waste limited visual capacity on query-irrelevant regions. We observe that effective grounding should prioritize observations that provide evidence for the query rather than uniformly represent the entire scene. Based on this insight, we introduce QVR3D, a query-guided visual reasoning framework that operates on RGB-D observations using off-the-shelf foundation models. QVR3D combines Query-Guided Maximum Coverage (QGMC) for selecting complementary query-relevant views with Grounding Probability Estimation (GPE) that integrates instance confidence, attribute consistency, and relationship consistency. The framework supports both single- and multi-object grounding without task-specific adaptation. Experiments on ScanRefer and Nr3D achieve state-of-the-art zero-shot performance, while QGMC also improves frame efficiency across multiple 3D vision-language tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/jwliao1209/QVR3D.

title: Scute: Exact Batched Serving for PEFT Adapters Beyond LoRA
shortTitle: Scute: Exact Batched Serving for PEFT Adapters Beyond LoRA
abstract: Existing serving systems for large language models batch requests for many different LoRA adapters on one GPU. However, these systems reject adapters from other parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as DoRA, (IA), VeRA and OFT. One solution to this is to convert these adapters to LoRA, but this induces a significant memory and accuracy cost. Instead, we show that, under some modifications, a batched LoRA kernel can serve all of these methods exactly and efficiently. We achieve this by writing each method in one normal form, a LoRA computation with six slots for an adapter's own vectors and matrices. Some slots can merge into an adapter's weights at load time; the others remain live and induce a cost. We give ways to efficiently pay this cost and predict it from a zero-parameter byte model. We package this system, Scute, and build it on top of vLLM. Scute serves all five methods, coming as checkpoints from the Hugging Face PEFT library, in one batch, and it matches that library with a mean error of at most 1.5% of each adapter's effect. Under a burst of requests on an RTX A6000, a mix of these methods takes 5-17% more decode time than the same number of LoRA adapters. Furthermore, using Scute, the same GPU can serve 64 to 1024 (IA) and VeRA adapters at 1.5x to at least 2.5x the request rate of their LoRA conversions.

title: Pop Goes the Verifier: Phoneme-Targeted Data Poisoning of Voice Liveness Detection
shortTitle: Pop Goes the Verifier: Phoneme-Targeted Data Poisoning of Voice Liveness Detection
abstract: Many Automated Speaker Verification Systems (ASVs) commonly employ liveliness detection techniques, such as VoicePop, which identify genuine speech by analyzing low- frequency pop bursts from plosive phonemes using Gammatone Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (GFCC) and an SVM classifier. While effective against traditional replay attacks, such systems are vulnerable to data poisoning techniques. Prior work shows that broadly applied SyntheticPop attacks can collapse model to accuracy to as low as 14.01% using only 20% poisoned samples, but the resulting artifacts are easily detectable when visualizing the waveform energies. This paper introduces Pop Goes the Verifier, a stealthier phoneme injection poisoning attack. By leveraging FastSpeech 2 (FS2) with a modified HiFi-GAN vocoder, we inject localized pop bursts at plosive phoneme locations and overlay subtle Gaussian noise to reduce the visibility of injected artifacts in waveform and spectrogram analysis. Using the ASVSpoof 2019 as the dataset, we observe that the approach achieves a moderate poisoning attack while providing greater resistance to signal-level inspection than the original SyntheticPop attack.

title: Digital Twin-Assisted Fast Beam Alignment for mmWave MIMO Networks
shortTitle: Digital Twin-Assisted Fast Beam Alignment for mmWave MIMO Networks
abstract: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) communication relies on directional beam sweeping for initial access, which incurs substantial latency and signaling overhead as antenna arrays grow large and deployments become denser. Machine-learning-based beam prediction can reduce this overhead, but its effectiveness depends on training data that accurately reflects the deployment environment, a requirement that is difficult to meet in practice. This paper presents a latency-aware beam management architecture that integrates digital-twin-assisted prediction, regionbased localization, weighted ensemble learning, and explainability-driven beam pruning into a unified framework. A digital twin (DT) generates site-specific ray-traced channel knowledge offline, enabling environment-aware beam prediction without exhaustive real-world measurements and supporting both initial access and beam tracking. The proposed ensemble learning scheme combines a base classifier and a specialist classifier through reliability-weighted fusion to improve prediction accuracy and robustness, while explainable artificial intelligence (XAI)-based attribution pruning reduces the beam codebook to a small subset of the most informative beams for beam allocation. To capture the distributional mismatch between the DT and real-world environments: the network was trained on imperfect digital-twin data but evaluated on real-world surrobase data. Results show that the proposed method achieves 96.80% top-1 and 98.36% top-3 beam prediction accuracy, while reducing over-the-air sounding overhead by nearly an order of magnitude relative to exhaustive sweeping, outperforming convolutional and deep neural network baselines from prior work.

title: Auriga Technical Report: A Task-Agnostic Agent Harness for Zero-Shot Embodied Manipulation
shortTitle: Auriga Technical Report: A Task-Agnostic Agent Harness for Zero-Shot Embodied Manipulation
abstract: Vision-language models can interpret instructions and plan manipulation tasks, yet struggle when acting directly as robot policies. On RoboDojo, a large planning-execution gap separates high-level task decisions from physical execution: removing arm execution raises GPT-6 Astra's success rate from 22.5% under the reference control interface to 76.2%. We present Auriga, a task-agnostic agent harness that closes 68.3% of this gap in zero-shot manipulation without target-task trials or resets. In Auriga, the model makes all task decisions over an explicit task belief and acts through either direct tool calls or synthesized multi-step Python programs, while the harness supplies calibrated 3D measurements, finger-referenced dual-arm control, and a single admission gateway to the robot. Before motion, the model inspects a visual trajectory preview while simulation is paused; during execution, the harness checks declared stage tolerances and grasp bounds, stopping the robot on divergence and returning the measured discrepancy for in-place recovery. Developed across 13 cross-task capability iterations and frozen for evaluation, Auriga ranks first on the RoboDojo leaderboard with a 57.7% success rate (64.0 Score), more than doubling the reference harness on the same model, and remains first under scene randomization while learned policies drop by up to 33.9%. On RoboCasa365, the same frozen harness reaches a 73.2% success rate, outperforming VLA-assisted agents by up to 23.1% on composite tasks. title: CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies
shortTitle: CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies
abstract: Can a language model learn better ways to reason about other people's minds by improving its own strategies, and are the strategies it learns actually right? We study this with cogrsi. A grounded reader marks who saw each event in a story and uses a short written principle to settle disagreements between its readings. With a principle written by experts, it beats self-consistency at the same token cost. A self-improvement loop then writes the principle itself. It keeps an update only if accuracy rises by a calibrated margin, and in one variant only if it also passes counterfactual test pairs. The learned principles transfer: on 800 BigToM pairs that no system had seen, each of them scores higher than the expert principle. We then check what the learned rules actually say. Each rule is translated into code and run on thousands of small stories with known answers. Most of them give a wrong answer in at least one situation they claim to cover, for example by treating a character who is in the room as knowing what happened even while asleep. Accuracy does not reveal which rules are wrong, and the counterfactual test does not fix this. A strategy can help in practice and still be wrong as a rule, so both need checking. Our code and data are publicly available.

title: CompSkill: Compiling Execution Experience for Skill Retrieval
shortTitle: CompSkill: Compiling Execution Experience for Skill Retrieval
abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on skill documents, yet most retrievers rank them by description alone and ignore what earlier executions revealed, even though a relevant skill can hurt execution. We present CompSkill, which indexes skills with learned 512-d keys and compiles matched same-task comparisons into skill offsets and capped key residuals (KeyOpt), so experience changes which document the executor receives, never its text. Under a logistic outcome model with unknown task difficulty, matched comparisons cancel that difficulty and only discordant ones carry information; on support executions, predictions improve with each discordant task. An experience hypergraph keeps each comparison with its executor and document versions, recalls missed skills and grounds a cited review. Compact keys raise SkillRet NDCG@10 from 64.0 to 70.9 at one eighth of the dimension. With one document, CompSkill completes 256 and 260 of 332 ToolQA tasks with GPT-5.6-luna and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, respectively, more than every baseline, and stays on par with the strongest baselines on AppWorld and ALFWorld. On 332 newly generated ToolQA tasks, it completes 256 with GPT-5.6-luna, significantly more than BM25, SkillRet-8B, Tool2Vec and RankGPT; over all 844 ToolQA tasks, it completes 24 more than the strongest baseline. Selection matters beyond relevance: pairing the right guide with a same-database sibling instead of another database's guide costs 8 of 96 tasks. Code, models and support data: https://github.com/satoshinji2992/CompSkill

title: Zero-Gated Cross-Attention
shortTitle: Zero-Gated Cross-Attention
abstract: Injecting non-text modalities into frozen language models often introduces early optimization instability, making it difficult to separate architectural gains from transient training dynamics. We introduce Inductively Gated Cross-Attention (IGCA), a zero-initialized cross-attention bridge that preserves pretrained model behavior at initialization while enabling gradual multimodal conditioning. Integrated across six decoder layers of frozen Falcon-40B, open_llama_30b, and Bloom-7b1 backbones (with 40,404,961,288 trainable adapter parameters used during training), IGCA acts as an exact algebraic no-op at initialization with a maximum output discrepancy of 0.00e+00. Over 59,500 training steps on Falcon-40B, the training loss decreases from 3.9403 to 0.0007 (with final ten step losses of [0.0001, 0.0003, 0.0005, 0.0002, 0.0005, 0.0011, 0.0005, 0.0006, 0.0005, 0.0007]). On held-out evaluation, the best gate-on checkpoint achieves a loss of 2.2201 compared to 4.3469 for the gate-off baseline -- a 48.9% reduction (2.1268 nats) -- while average held-out loss improves from 4.3423 to 2.2498 (1.9075 nats) with a mean gate magnitude of $\vert{}\tanh(α)\vert{} = 0.0713$.

title: StreamDuo: A Live Commentator and a Research Agent for Unseen Games
shortTitle: StreamDuo: A Live Commentator and a Research Agent for Unseen Games
abstract: Streaming video LLMs can now commentate live gameplay, but they are trained and tested on the same games. We study cross-game streaming commentary, in which a model trained on one game commentates games it has never seen, and find that current commentators transfer their timing but not their knowledge of the game world. We propose StreamDuo, which pairs a trainable commentator with a frozen research agent that reads the wiki of the game being played. When the commentator sees something it cannot name, it sends the current frames, and the research agent returns a few wiki entries two seconds later while the stream continues. We train only the commentator, on a single game, in two stages. Information-gain labels teach it to ask only where an answer would help it say what the human caster said, and on-policy self-distillation from a copy of itself that sees the ideal answer teaches it to use noisy answers. Trained on Baldur's Gate 3 and tested on ten unseen games, StreamDuo raises entity recall from 0.082 to 0.116 over Proact-VL trained on the same data, cuts source-game leakage from 9.9% to 1.0%, and achieves the best timing and the highest judged liveliness and overall quality among streaming models.

title: Do Earnings Calls Help Predict Financial Restatements? Evaluating Text Beyond Public Firm Information
shortTitle: Do Earnings Calls Help Predict Financial Restatements? Evaluating Text Beyond Public Firm Information
abstract: Financial restatements correct errors in previously published financial reports. Could managers' language in earnings calls warn of them in advance? Comparing 109 calls that precede restatements with 218 matched control calls, we find that the text predicts restatements but adds no detectable ranking gain beyond public firm information. A text classifier beats chance, largely because of restatements tied to special-purpose acquisition companies, but a model using only public information scores slightly higher. With refitting, the 95% interval for the gain from adding text (-0.05 to 0.11 AUROC) still leaves room for a meaningful benefit. A large language model scores higher, but we show that it names the exact ticker in 66% of masked transcripts, and it was released after the restatements occurred. Our results suggest that finding new warning signs in call text requires a public-information baseline and a check of what a language model already knows.

title: What Does a Safety Label Measure? Auditing Situational-Safety Benchmarks for Multimodal LLMs
shortTitle: What Does a Safety Label Measure? Auditing Situational-Safety Benchmarks for Multimodal LLMs
abstract: Situational-safety benchmarks label each scene SAFE or UNSAFE and score a multimodal large language model (MLLM) against that label, usually by judging its free-form answer, and these scores guide deployment. We ask what such a label measures. A label score can come from the scene, the request or the benchmark's own files. We propose the Benchmark Card, seven measured fields that tell them apart, and fill it for six benchmarks. Only MSSBench chat leaks the label through its image files: image size alone reaches 82.3% accuracy, matching or beating six of seven commercial models. Elsewhere the signal outside the scene comes from design. In MOSSBench the item partition fixes the label, and on HoliSafe the request alone ranks pairs about as well as the scene. On our corrected chat split, the size rule falls to chance. We then introduce the Spot-Stop decomposition, which compares ranking with labelling on pairs of a safe and an unsafe scene. It splits the gap above a label-swap null into three parts: a threshold part, overlap between safe and unsafe scores, and order that holds only within a pair. Most of fourteen open MLLMs rank better than they label, beyond what their AUROC predicts. On chat, one shared threshold repairs a third to a half of the excess, and label-free recentering recovers it on balanced batches. Recentering on unlabelled scenes of the same situation improves ranking on VSCBench for 13 of 14 models.

title: HiGenTrans: Hierarchical LLM Knowledge Transfer for Generative Recommendation
shortTitle: HiGenTrans: Hierarchical LLM Knowledge Transfer for Generative Recommendation
abstract: Generative recommendation promises to simplify conventional multi-stage recommender systems by generating item Semantic IDs (SIDs) autoregressively. However, two obstacles limit its effective- ness in industrial settings: interaction-only supervision underuses the semantic knowledge encoded in pretrained language models, while beam-search likelihood ranks token sequences rather than directly estimating item relevance. To address these limitations, we propose HiGenTrans, a three-level framework that introduces LLM knowledge at the input, representation, and decision levels. First, Global Semantic Priming (GSP) adds an LLM-derived user representation to the beginning-of-sequence embedding, provid- ing a semantic prior before SID generation. Second, Hierarchi- cal Representation Transfer (HRT) aligns intermediate LLM representations with depth-matched GenRec layers through mean- centered projections and gated residual connections. Finally, Multi- Signal Decision Calibration (MDC) uses a lightweight mixture- of-experts calibrator to combine semantic relevance, generation confidence, and candidate-set context when reranking beam-search outputs. All semantic features are computed only from the observ- able interaction prefix, preventing target leakage, and can be cached offline. Experiments on three public benchmarks show that HiGen- Trans improves Recall@10 by up to 12.9% and NDCG@10 by up to 33.7% over the strongest baselines. These results demonstrate the value of transferring LLM knowledge at complementary stages of the generative recommendation pipeline.

title: Rethinking LLM Pruning via Test-Time Scaling
shortTitle: Rethinking LLM Pruning via Test-Time Scaling
abstract: Structured pruning reduces the size of large language models, often at the cost of lower accuracy. Whether this decline reflects diminished reasoning capacity or greater difficulty in sampling correct solutions is less clear. We examine this question across expert, FFN and layer pruning on four mathematical and coding benchmarks, comparing original and pruned models through pass@k at matched sampling budgets. Even after substantial pruning, some models match or exceed the original model's reasoning coverage despite lower pass@1, and solve problems left unsolved in the original samples. Retaining broad coverage, however, does not mean that correct solutions remain easy to obtain. Under severe pruning, diverse generated chain-of-thought (CoT) traces can coexist with increased repetition and less reliable generation. As correct answers become harder to sample, the additional attempts can sharply increase total token use even when individual responses become shorter. This separation between coverage and sampling efficiency also clarifies expert-selection gains, as methods with markedly different pass@1 can solve the same problems at large budgets yet require different numbers of attempts to reach a common coverage target. Pruning should therefore be assessed by both the range of problems a model can still solve and the sampling cost of obtaining correct solutions.

title: Compile as Hypothesis: A Headroom Typology for Prompt Optimization on Real Reasoning Models
shortTitle: Compile as Hypothesis: A Headroom Typology for Prompt Optimization on Real Reasoning Models
abstract: Automated prompt compilers search for or rewrite prompts under the implicit assumption that optimization consistently improves downstream task performance. We evaluate this assumption on frontier reasoning models through rigorous paired, same-day measurements. Across four optimizer families (genome search, profile-guided mutation, GEPA, and ESPO) and eight tasks, structured search yields no statistically significant accuracy gains on strong reasoners. However, a discrete structural genome provides essential architectural stability, preventing catastrophic bimodal seed-collapse (where unconstrained search collapses toward the judge floor in 3/5 runs). Through 190-problem evaluations on knowledge-intensive benchmarks, we establish a three-dimensional headroom typology: prompt optimization cannot compensate for intrinsic knowledge deficits or physical token truncation, but successfully resolves protocol and formatting errors. On gpt-6, while free-text reflective search (GEPA) yields a +.14 gain on a task where structured search remains flat, qualitative ablation reveals that ~.035 stems from judge-rubric reconstruction while ~.105 reflects genuine instruction refinement. Our pre-registered AutoAPC-Select deployment gate matches the oracle policy in 5/7 groups and rescues seed-collapse arms with zero regret. Finally, we expose silent backend-mixing in commercial APIs during outage windows and provide automated per-call audit verification tools to ensure empirical evaluation fidelity.

title: SIDRec: End-to-End Semantic ID Representation and Modeling for Recommendation
shortTitle: SIDRec: End-to-End Semantic ID Representation and Modeling for Recommendation
abstract: Semantic IDs (SIDs) have emerged as a promising approach for discriminative recommendation by encoding continuous item rep- resentations into compact discrete identifiers. However, existing SID-based methods face two fundamental limitations: semantic mis- match between content semantics and collaborative preferences, and objective mismatch between SID construction and downstream recommendation optimization. To address these challenges, we propose SIDRec, an end-to-end recommendation-aware SID learn- ing framework that jointly models content and collaborative in- formation while aligning SID construction with recommendation objectives. Specifically, SIDRec introduces a self-updating fusion mechanism that explicitly integrates pretrained content represen- tations with collaborative embeddings initialized from a trained recommendation model, enabling preference-aware semantic mod- eling. Furthermore, SIDRec employs an MMoE-inspired joint opti- mization mechanism with shared experts and task-specific gates, allowing recommendation supervision to directly guide differen- tiable quantization and produce task-adaptive discrete representa- tions. Extensive experiments on three public benchmark datasets demonstrate that SIDRec consistently outperforms all competing methods across both AUC and GAUC, achieving up to 5.15% relative improvements over the strongest baselines. Further ablation stud- ies validate the effectiveness and complementarity of collaborative semantic modeling and end-to-end SID optimization.

title: GESTALT: Fast, Generalizable Histopathology Image Synthesis from Gene Expression with Pretrained Pathology Foundation Models
shortTitle: GESTALT: Fast, Generalizable Histopathology Image Synthesis from Gene Expression with Pretrained Pathology Foundation Models
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics measures gene expression while preserving where each cell sits in the tissue. The inverse, what a given transcriptomic state looks like, is less explored but equally useful: it lets researchers visualize the morphological consequence of a molecular state and interpret a spatial assay's molecular calls against real tissue structure. GeneFlow, the current state of the art on the Xenium gene expression-to-image benchmark, trains a model from scratch, incurring a high cost on every new target dataset it is applied to. We instead propose GESTALT, which reformulates gene expression-to-image synthesis as predicting a pathology foundation model's image embedding. A lightweight gene-token transformer predicts this embedding from multi-cell gene expression, and a frozen or LoRA-adapted diffusion decoder (PixCell) renders it as an image. Because this visual knowledge is reused rather than relearned, GESTALT trains in a fraction of the time. In both multi-cell and single-cell settings, our method outperforms the SoTA on perceptual metrics across all three Xenium datasets. Beyond improved image quality, GESTALT natively synthesizes at 1024 x 1024, and is evaluated in three generalization settings: zero-shot transfer across gene panels and datasets, held-out patients and disease states, and transfer across studies and tissue sources. Coupled with a statistical model of spatial expression, GESTALT also provides, to our knowledge, the first paired synthesis of cell-resolved transcriptomic fields and tissue images with explicit control over cell type, density, and composition. Code is available at https://github.com/trongnhandev1011/Gestalt.

title: GSLM2: Multi-Stream Speech Representation Learning and Generative Spoken Language Modeling
shortTitle: GSLM2: Multi-Stream Speech Representation Learning and Generative Spoken Language Modeling
abstract: Generative spoken language models (SLMs) offer a route to learning linguistic structure purely from speech, yet they lag far behind text-based models in both capability and data scaling efficiency. We identify two bottlenecks underlying this gap: the limited linguistic quality of existing speech units and the reliance on a single stream of discrete units to represent speech. Multiple codebooks are widely used to encode acoustic features but rarely to represent speech semantics. We present GSLM2, which learns and models complementary properties of speech at multiple levels of abstraction. Its encoder, SpidR 2.0, uses self-supervised learning with differentiable prediction heads to induce high-quality discrete units at multiple levels. A multi-stream SLM then jointly models these units using a shared temporal backbone, stream-specific predictors, and an autoregressive head that captures cross-stream dependencies. Across training data sizes and model scales, up to 6M hours and 6.5B parameters, GSLM2 consistently improves linguistic competence while scaling more efficiently with data. As a result, it substantially narrows the gap between spoken and text-based LMs; across read and conversational speech domains, we shrink the gap by about two orders of magnitude on sWuggy, sBLIMP, and tSC, while also outperforming competitive speech-text systems on all three tasks. We open-source the training code and model checkpoints at https://github.com/facebookresearch/gslm2.

title: CivicBench: A Benchmark and Memory Framework for Web-Based Civic Data Analytics
shortTitle: CivicBench: A Benchmark and Memory Framework for Web-Based Civic Data Analytics
abstract: Municipalities publish service requests, geographic boundaries, weather observations, demographic estimates, and operational guidance through independently maintained Web portals. Civic analysis must combine these sources while preserving their schemas, source links, spatial and temporal scopes, and interpretive limits. Tool-using language agents can perform this integration, but existing task benchmarks rarely test whether a computed claim remains supported by the records used. We present CivicBench, a 400-task benchmark over four cities and two years that materializes civic Web data into frozen bundles for reproducible evaluation. Executable contracts score computation, source linkage, coverage, scope, qualified answers, and refusal when the requested conclusion is not supported. We also introduce Task-State Memory (TSM), which compiles tool observations into typed assertions, reconciles records only within compatible scopes, and retrieves a bounded state organized around unresolved constraints. Across nine completed model pairs, eight yield positive mean-score differences with 95\% semantic-contract-cluster bootstrap intervals excluding zero; the ninth interval crosses zero. The benchmark and memory framework make the records behind a claim inspectable at the point of decision.

title: Capacity Planning for Resource-Constrained Clinical LLM Serving
shortTitle: Capacity Planning for Resource-Constrained Clinical LLM Serving
abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) under a fixed accelerator budget requires jointly deciding how computational capacity is allocated across model sizes and how incoming requests are routed across that capacity. Although prior work has extensively studied LLM routing and serving efficiency, the relative importance of fleet composition and routing under resource constraints remains less understood. We investigate this question using a controlled four-GPU serving environment with heterogeneous clinical NLP workloads spanning short factual verification, biomedical semantic matching, and long-context clinical summarization. We systematically vary fleet composition, routing policy, and offered load while holding the workload trace and hardware budget fixed. Across 24 configurations, descriptive main-effect shares attribute more variation to fleet composition than to the evaluated routing policies in time to first token, latency, and long-context coverage. All-small fleets provide the best responsiveness and throughput but substantially lower long-context coverage, whereas larger-model capacity improves coverage at the cost of serving efficiency. Heterogeneous fleets provide intermediate operating points but can introduce strong-model bottlenecks when large-model capacity is scarce. In a focused evaluation of this bottleneck, capacity-aware routing reduces mean latency and increases throughput while incurring a small reduction in long-context coverage. Within this measured regime, the results support prioritizing capacity allocation, with routing managing demand within the provisioned capacity.

title: Lower Bounds on Inference Complexity for Polyak-Ruppert Averaged Stochastic Gradient Descent
shortTitle: Lower Bounds on Inference Complexity for Polyak-Ruppert Averaged Stochastic Gradient Descent
abstract: In this paper, we establish sharp lower bounds for Gaussian approximation of Polyak-Ruppert averaged stochastic gradient descent with polynomially decreasing step sizes. For every fixed exponent $γ\in(1/2,1)$, a single one-dimensional smooth, strongly convex example has approximation error with the limiting variance of order $n^{1/2-γ}+n^{γ-1}$ in Kolmogorov and convex distances. This matches the existing upper bound throughout the range of $γ$. The nonlinear bias contributes $n^{1/2-γ}$ even when the Gaussian reference uses the finite linearized variance. We also derive a lower bound of order $n^{-(1-γ)/2}$ for the relative mean error of estimating the limiting variance from one SGD trajectory, uniformly over a scalar quadratic family. With the limiting variance known, achieving approximation error $\varepsilon$ on this example takes order $\varepsilon^{-4}$ iterations for the best choice $γ=3/4$. Achieving both Gaussian approximation and relative mean variance-estimation errors at most $\varepsilon$ uniformly over the model class requires at least order $\varepsilon^{-6}$ iterations for every fixed $γ$.

title: SHield: Watermarking 4D Gaussian Splatting via Spherical Harmonic Coefficient Perturbation
shortTitle: SHield: Watermarking 4D Gaussian Splatting via Spherical Harmonic Coefficient Perturbation
abstract: 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) models are computationally expensive to train but distributed as easily copied parameter files. Existing watermarks protect these assets by fine-tuning the scene against a neural decoder to extract bit strings from rendered video, a heavy process vulnerable to the temporal dynamics of dynamic scenes. However, if the threat model targets the redistributed file itself, verification can be vastly simplified. Because the canonical Spherical-Harmonic (SH) coefficients of 4DGS are time- and view-invariant, parameter-space perturbations can be recovered via deterministic arithmetic. We propose **SHield**, the first non-blind, decoder-free watermarking approach that natively embeds full-resolution RGB images into 4DGS files. SHield tiles a zero-mean payload across the SH coefficients of a key-selected Gaussian subset, applying a brief anchored optimization to preserve visual fidelity. To verify ownership, it geometrically re-associates the key using canonical Gaussian centres to survive file tampering and recovers the payload in closed form. Across 30 scenes (D-NeRF, HyperNeRF, DyNeRF), SHield guarantees near-perfect payload recovery (Pearson $r \geq 0.991$) on all 150 tested models with a mean rendering penalty of $\leq 0.13$~dB. Held-out evaluation yields perfect detection on 400 true trials and zero false positives across $1{,}600$ wrong-subset null trials. We also strictly bound the method's robustness: SHield survives INT8 quantization and $30\%$ opacity pruning for the image payload, and on aggressive SH-degree-1 truncation bit payloads are still decodable.

title: Lightweight Representation Learning for Low Tucker Rank Tensors
shortTitle: Lightweight Representation Learning for Low Tucker Rank Tensors
abstract: Low Tucker rank tensors provide compact representations of multidimensional dependencies, but standard learning pipelines can incur substantial computational and memory overhead from redundant intermediate quantities. We reduce this overhead without modifying the underlying representation objective or parameterization. Our approach combines three complementary components: (i) sequential extraction of only task-required spectral components, avoiding unnecessary full decompositions; (ii) factor-wise multilinear contractions without materializing large Kronecker operators; and (iii) compact latent-state updates without storing full ambient tensor iterates. These components preserve the algebraic operations and learning trajectories of the original algorithms while reducing their computational and memory footprints. Across five low Tucker rank tensor estimators, our implementations match the original trajectories to numerical precision (relative discrepancies of $10^{-16}$ to $10^{-13}$), while reducing per-iteration runtime by up to $3.12\times$ and resident memory by up to $616\times$ ($99.8\%$) on the main order-3 benchmark at $n=100$, with memory reductions exceeding $900\times$ across the full evaluation suite. These results show that substantial computational redundancy can be eliminated from Tucker representation learning without changing the underlying model or learned representation.

title: Concept-Guided Prompting Strategies Increase Diversity in LLM-Generated Recipe Populations
shortTitle: Concept-Guided Prompting Strategies Increase Diversity in LLM-Generated Recipe Populations
abstract: Novelty in solution generation supports automated discovery, but LLM outputs can remain repetitive. Concept-guided prompting outperformed both baselines in all cases and reached semantic coverage of 47.0% versus 35.1% and 13.1% in respective prior-title and nonce prompt strategies. These findings suggest broader population exploration and diversity, but remain contained to this specific task. Further work is needed to determine the quality of solutions and generalizability.

title: TRIAGE: Reliability- and Load-Conditioned Escalation for Two-Tier LLM Serving with a Semantic Evidence Judge
shortTitle: TRIAGE: Reliability- and Load-Conditioned Escalation for Two-Tier LLM Serving with a Semantic Evidence Judge
abstract: Two-tier LLM serving escalates selected requests from a small model to a large one, but prompt-based routers cannot see whether retrieved evidence supports an answer, and they treat the GPU cost of an escalation as constant. title: Benchmark Study for Quantum Statevector Simulators for Scientific Computing
shortTitle: Benchmark Study for Quantum Statevector Simulators for Scientific Computing
abstract: Quantum circuit simulators are essential for quantum algorithm development, yet systematic runtime benchmarks comparing major frameworks across CPU and GPU backends are limited. We benchmark three open-source frameworks - Cirq (qsim), CUDA-Q, and Qiskit (Aer) - on statevector simulation of the 2D quantum acoustic wave equation, evolved via Trotterized Hamiltonian dynamics, for problem sizes from 7 to 29 qubits on a single Azure virtual machine. The evaluation spans four categories: CPU runtime versus qubit count, strong scalability on multi-core CPUs at 27 qubits, GPU runtime versus qubit count, and GPU-over-CPU speedup. Relative rankings shift from one category to the next. On CPU, Cirq is fastest up to 23 qubits (2.4x faster than Qiskit at 21 qubits), but Qiskit overtakes it at larger sizes and higher thread counts, sustaining 80% parallel efficiency at 16 threads. On GPU, CUDA-Q leads between 13 and 21 qubits, while Cirq becomes the fastest GPU backend at large problem sizes, achieving 1.5x and 2.3x speedups over CUDA-Q and Qiskit at 29 qubits. GPU-over-CPU speedup ratios should be interpreted alongside absolute GPU runtimes; CUDA-Q's 1500x at 21 qubits is largely driven by the limited scaling of its CPU backend (qpp), and the absolute GPU runtimes show that the three frameworks' GPU backends differ by less than these ratios alone suggest. These results indicate that no single framework dominates across configurations, and that backend selection for statevector simulation should be guided by both target hardware and problem size.

title: Fast and Exact Relative-Position Attention via Structure-Aware Kernels
shortTitle: Fast and Exact Relative-Position Attention via Structure-Aware Kernels
abstract: Relative-position attention mechanisms offer compelling alternatives to RoPE across various transformer architectures, delivering superior performance in domains such as audio. These mechanisms typically modify attention scores by adding content-position or bias-position terms. Unlike RoPE, which encodes position via per-token rotations directly on the queries and keys, relative-position terms generally require pairwise offset-dependent computation or lookups, complicating their integration into fused attention kernels and introducing severe memory, bandwidth, and compute overheads as sequences scale. To address this bottleneck, we propose an exact attention algorithm that incorporates additive relative-position terms into FlashAttention-style tiled computation. Our method (1) uses offset-aware tiling to avoid redundant indexing and memory accesses, (2) computes only the necessary key/query-relation products and reuses them across token pairs in both forward and backward passes, and (3) uses offset-based gradient sharding and aggregation, eliminating atomic contention. We provide a unified, efficient Triton implementation across diverse relative-position attention mechanisms and evaluate it against naive and specialized implementations. For 8K-token sequences, our method speeds up the forward (backward) pass by 1.8-6.4$\times$ (2.0-21$\times$) and reduces peak memory up to 2.9-128$\times$ (1.4-54$\times$) over the strongest baseline for each mechanism, enabling long-context end-to-end transcription that is 1.8$\times$ faster and uses 2.4$\times$ less memory. Our method thus provides a drop-in, hardware-efficient solution for scaling relative-position attention transformers.

title: Satisfied, Not Solving: Wireheading of Bounded Homeostatic Rewards in Reinforcement Learning
shortTitle: Satisfied, Not Solving: Wireheading of Bounded Homeostatic Rewards in Reinforcement Learning

We test this for a homeostatic satiation reward, in which needs build up and relieving them is rewarding, and give the agent a cheap action that resets its needs. In MiniGrid DoorKey-8x8, PPO agents with this action solved 2 of 80 seeds, against 71 of 80 on the same seeds without it; in KeyCorridorS3R1, 0 of 20 against 20 of 20. Their policies stayed near uniform. The reward does not ask for this: a telescoping argument caps any policy's satiation return at the needs' starting drive, and a post-hoc computation shows that, at every growth rate we trained, a solving trajectory beats that cap on all sampled layouts. In DoorKey with advantage normalization on, a satisfaction signal the agent could fill itself was worse than none (11 of 20 solved with task reward alone, 1 of 20 with the tamperable signal), and a per-press cost of 0.1 restored the task in every seed. Farming of positive reward cycles appeared in DoorKey but not persistently in KeyCorridorS3R1. All predictions were pre-registered, and hash-locked from round 3 on; 9 of our 23 hypotheses were not supported, and we report each.

title: Zeroth-Order Policy Optimization for Scheduling in Queueing Networks
shortTitle: Zeroth-Order Policy Optimization for Scheduling in Queueing Networks
abstract: Reinforcement learning in queueing network scheduling presents significant challenges because of the countably infinite state space and the high stochasticity in transitions. In this paper, we propose zeroth-order policy optimization algorithms that are easy to implement and rely solely on estimates of the average cost, a single scalar quantity, without requiring the estimation of value or advantage functions. Our analysis focuses on back-pressure guarded policies and establishes uniform smoothness of the average cost objective with respect to the policy parameters. Building on this property, we establish finite-time convergence guarantees to an $ε$-stationary policy for the proposed algorithms. Numerical experiments on multiple queueing networks, including systems beyond classical exponential service distribution, demonstrate competitive performance, outperforming gradient-based RL methods like PPO and traditional queueing baselines.

title: Stochastic Summaries: Characterizing Structured Datasets Using Probabilistic Programs
shortTitle: Stochastic Summaries: Characterizing Structured Datasets Using Probabilistic Programs
abstract: What does my data look like? We study the problem of representing and learning summaries of datasets that account for both their structural and statistical properties. This problem is widely useful across many application domains that involve large datasets and analysis/modeling of data, and is of particular interest to Programming Languages. In particular, in this work we focus on the problem of learning these "stochastic summaries" for tree-like data composed of inductive datatypes and argue that probabilistic programs over inductive datatypes can effectively represent the desired summaries. We present Tali, a Probabilistic Programming Language over inductive datatypes, and study the problem of learning such programs from data samples. We identify a semantic property, called Observation-Bounded Compilability, which identifies a set of recursive probabilistic programs which admit exact inference, and can represent many useful and complex probabilistic structures. We then propose an algorithm for learning Tali programs satisfying the OBC property from observations using a combination of program synthesis (stochastic search) and maximum likelihood inference. We implement our learning framework, evaluate it on a diverse benchmark suite, and record our observations on the merits of our approach. We demonstrate the utility of learning stochastic summaries as symbolically-represented priors for downstream learning tasks. We also showcase another utility by using our technique to learn operational profiles of real-world datasets.

title: ClothDojo: Learned Data Generation and Benchmarking for Bimanual Garment Flattening and Folding
shortTitle: ClothDojo: Learned Data Generation and Benchmarking for Bimanual Garment Flattening and Folding

title: ArSciKids: Arabic Curriculum-Aligned Datasets for Scientific Experiment and Multiple-Choice Question Generation in Primary Education
shortTitle: ArSciKids: Arabic Curriculum-Aligned Datasets for Scientific Experiment and Multiple-Choice Question Generation in Primary Education

title: Online Autotuning of Algebraic Multigrid via Contextual Bandits and Reinforcement Learning
shortTitle: Online Autotuning of Algebraic Multigrid via Contextual Bandits and Reinforcement Learning

A recursive LSTDQ controller uses residual and timing observations to estimate the AMG solve time within each attempt and adapt relaxation weights between multigrid cycles. title: Learning Agile Humanoid Dodgeball with Onboard Monocular Vision
shortTitle: Learning Agile Humanoid Dodgeball with Onboard Monocular Vision

title: GraCo: A Unified Toolkit of Graph Coarsening Algorithms and Metrics
shortTitle: GraCo: A Unified Toolkit of Graph Coarsening Algorithms and Metrics
abstract: Graph coarsening aims to reduce a graph to a smaller one that preserves chosen properties of the original. It is increasingly used to scale graph learning to large graphs, as a non-differentiable step applied once before training. Many coarsening methods have been proposed in recent years, each with its own implementation, notation and evaluation. In this work, we introduce GraCo, a unified toolkit of graph coarsening methods. It relies on a single definition: a coarsening is fixed by a partition of the nodes and by the Laplacian the coarsened graph is consistent with. The coarsened graph, and the reduction and lifting matrices that map signals from the original graph to the coarsened one and back, follow from these two choices. We implement 17 methods from the literature and a random baseline, grouped into five families, with the same notation, inputs and outputs. We also build a collection of metrics from different papers, applicable to any coarsening. We check the implementations on a synthetic stochastic block model, then we report the runtime and peak memory of each method on Cora, PubMed, ogbn-arxiv and ogbn-products. title: Vision-Language Models Are Joint Denoisers in Robotic Action Generation
shortTitle: Vision-Language Models Are Joint Denoisers in Robotic Action Generation
abstract: Diffusion-based vision-language-action (VLA) models cascade pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) with diffusion action experts, but typically restrict the VLM to providing static conditioning. This separation limits how much pretrained perception and reasoning can guide action generation, especially in out-of-distribution settings. We introduce JADE, a Joint Action DEnoiser that enables the VLM and action expert to jointly refine actions. Our key insight is that structured action latents allow the VLM to read the current noisy action together with visual observations and language instructions. At every denoising step, the VLM contextualizes the noisy action and guides the action expert through gated cross-attention, so that its guidance evolves with the action being generated. We further supervise the VLM to recover clean action latents from noisy ones, which gives it a direct action-learning signal and couples perception with control. Additionally, joint denoising enables JADE to generate actions with fewer sampling steps, helping offset the additional cost of VLM participation. An adaptive step-size schedule further balances task performance and inference latency. On RoboDojo, JADE achieves an average success rate of 12.67%, the highest among the evaluated $π_{0.5}$-based methods, and is competitive with recent VLA and WAM foundation models pretrained at scale. title: Differentiable Iterative Learning Control for Black-Box Position-Commanded Manipulators
shortTitle: Differentiable Iterative Learning Control for Black-Box Position-Commanded Manipulators

At each trial, a constrained quadratic program computes a feasible command correction, while a real-anchored next-trial prediction defines a task-level objective. Hypergradients are obtained by implicitly differentiating the locally active KKT system, enabling multiple computational parameter updates without additional robot executions. Experiments on a 6-DoF DOBOT CR3 across unseen planar and three-dimensional trajectories show substantially faster physical-trial convergence than fixed-parameter model-based ILC. Across the four primary trajectories, after only two trial-to-trial updates, Diff-ILC achieves 78.8% and 76.4% lower mean joint-vector and Cartesian RMSE, respectively, than fixed-parameter model-based ILC.

title: Modeling Fat-shift for Improved Head Segmentation from MRI Scans using a Probabilistic Model
shortTitle: Modeling Fat-shift for Improved Head Segmentation from MRI Scans using a Probabilistic Model
abstract: Personalized computational head models for biophysical simulations rely on accurate whole-head segmentations from T1-weighted (T1w) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans. While T1w scans provide excellent contrast for intracranial anatomy, extracerebral tissues have partly almost no signal (compact bone) and also suffer from the so-called chemical shift artifact, which affects the fatty tissues in MRI and causes them to spatially shift in the frequency encoding direction of the scan. This artifact occurs primarily in two structures of the head: the spongy bone, a fatty compartment inside the compact bone, and the subcutaneous fat, located directly underneath the skin. The frequency-encoding direction is often set in the superior-inferior direction, causing the fatty tissues to shift down and, as a result, making the skull appear thinner than it actually is. Existing segmentation methods do not model this artifact, consequently leading to inaccurate labeling of the skull and scalp, which introduces a bias in biophysical simulations. The direction and magnitude of the fat-shift can be determined from the scan parameters, thus making it possible to explicitly model the shift and to recover the correct anatomy. This study introduces a probabilistic model that uses variational inference to segment head and brain structures from a T1w scan while accounting for the fat-shift artifact. The proposed Fat-shift-informed Label Optimization of the Whole head (FLOW) method reconstructs extracerebral anatomy more accurately than a fat-shift-agnostic segmentation approach while maintaining high segmentation accuracy in all other structures. FLOW-based fat-shift corrected segmentations significantly reduce bias in electric field simulations compared to a segmentation method that does not model the shift.

title: Reproducing INP-Former: Reconstructing Intrinsic Normal Prototypes for Industrial Anomaly Detection
shortTitle: Reproducing INP-Former: Reconstructing Intrinsic Normal Prototypes for Industrial Anomaly Detection
abstract: We reproduce the central claims of INP-Former, a reconstruction-based method for multi-class industrial anomaly detection. INP-Former extracts Intrinsic Normal Prototypes (INPs) from each test image and uses them to guide a decoder that reconstructs normal features, without a stored memory bank. Using the authors' released code, we reproduce the reported performance on MVTec AD and VisA and extend the evaluation to MVTec AD 2, where image AUROC with the default settings is 63.4, compared with 99.7 on MVTec AD. On MVTec AD, a five-seed ablation shows that most of the performance comes from the INP mechanism, while the two auxiliary losses add small changes whose direction depends on the metric. A paired comparison with both losses disabled confirms the benefit of INP on MVTec AD 2. The default of six prototypes transfers less well: the plateau beyond four prototypes reproduces on MVTec AD and VisA, but on MVTec AD 2 a single prototype outperforms six in AU-PRO on the public split and on both hidden test splits. We also measure practical trade-offs in resolution, backbone size, training length, and LoRA adaptation, and examine performance by defect size, lighting condition, and a stricter AU-PRO limit. Several conclusions from the original benchmarks, including the default prototype count, do not carry over to harder data. Code: https://github.com/garasnote/Repro-INPFormer

title: STLT: A Novel System for Energy-Aware Distributed Inference in the Edge-Cloud-Space Continuum
shortTitle: STLT: A Novel System for Energy-Aware Distributed Inference in the Edge-Cloud-Space Continuum
abstract: Low Earth Orbit satellites are pivotal for Earth observation tasks such as wildfire detection, capturing imagery for analysis by Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). On-board analysis reduces downlink volume, but severe energy constraints force a trade-off between computation and data transmission. Splitting the DNN between satellite and ground turns this balance into a design choice, where the split point determines combined computation and downlink energy. Existing approaches typically rely on static split-point decisions that fail to account for dynamic space conditions, or on complex algorithms, historical data, or prediction models that introduce significant overhead. To address these shortcomings, we present STLT, a two-stage system for energy-aware distributed inference between LEO satellites and a ground station. First, an offline analyzer characterizes the DNN architecture to identify a set of favorable split points, consequently reducing the search space. Second, an on-board algorithm performs lightweight energy-aware split selection, dynamically choosing from this pre-computed set based on the current state of the environment. We evaluate STLT on a real-world satellite telemetry dataset, showing that it reduces the split-candidate search space by 30.7% on average, lowers decision latency by 25.1% and energy by 27.5% on average, and delivers up to 20.1% more inference tasks than a state-of-the-art satellite-ground co-inference baseline while consuming 8.8% less energy overall.

title: Learning What to Ask and What to Believe: Distilling a Variational Bayesian Agent into Language Models
shortTitle: Learning What to Ask and What to Believe: Distilling a Variational Bayesian Agent into Language Models
abstract: Interactive tasks such as eliciting a user's preferences or diagnosing a hidden mechanism require an agent to track its uncertainty over a latent state, ask informative questions and act on the answers. Language models have no explicit mechanism for this, whereas Bayesian information seeking provides one through posterior inference and expected information gain (EIG), and we ask whether it can be distilled into an 8B language model. Our teacher, a lightweight Bayesian agent with a sequential variational belief and EIG query selection, matches or approaches exact and particle references on three task families. We generate synthetic interactions with the teacher on episodes disjoint from the benchmark and fine-tune \Student{} to reproduce its queries and its belief state as a structured scratchpad. On three Multi-Turn Puzzles tasks the student raises Circuit Decoding from 0.00 to 0.93 success, lowers the normalized rank of the recommended film from 0.50 to 0.10 and cuts word guessing from 32 to 3.4 attempts, exceeding the strongest reported language models on the two comparable tasks. Exposing the belief state closes much of the gap where the decision is an implicit computation rather than a read-out of the interaction; in matched teacher contrasts, EIG supervision consistently outperforms random querying, whereas greater inference fidelity does not uniformly improve the distilled student; a 70B language-model teacher does not match the Bayesian teacher in downstream student performance, and the learned skill does not transfer to an unseen task family. Variational Bayesian information seeking can thus be amortized into a language model by transferring the belief state that drives its questions and decisions.

title: Shades of Success: Evaluating Manipulation Quality from Object-Centric Constraints
shortTitle: Shades of Success: Evaluating Manipulation Quality from Object-Centric Constraints
abstract: As learned manipulation policies become increasingly capable of solving practical manipulation tasks, assessing how well a task is performed becomes a fundamental challenge. While binary labels confirm task success, they cannot distinguish successful executions with different levels of geometric precision. To address this, we introduce SPECTRA, an object-centric framework for quantifying execution quality in manipulation of rigid objects. From a small set of oracle demonstrations generated in simulation, SPECTRA represents object interactions through progress-aligned relative poses. SPECTRA identifies which relative-pose directions are constrained and their admissible variations from demonstrations. These constraints establish a reference for evaluating robotic manipulation tasks. To score an unseen execution, deviations beyond the admissible variation are summarized by a Task Quality Index Q in [0,1]. Across seven simulated tasks, SPECTRA recovers constraints with 94% accuracy using 30 demonstrations per task. On rollouts from three learned policies, its scores achieve pooled Spearman correlations with human judgments of p=0.81 over all rollouts and p=0.61 among successful rollouts, exceeding all baselines in both subsets. Using the task reference learned in simulation, we use SPECTRA to select the highest-scoring demonstrations for training a diffusion policy on hardware. Exploratory results show higher success rate than training on randomly selected demonstrations.

title: Context-Shielded Backdoor Attack against Large Vision-Language Models
shortTitle: Context-Shielded Backdoor Attack against Large Vision-Language Models
abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) routinely use inference-time visual-token compression to prune hundreds of patch tokens down to a compact budget. Existing LVLM backdoors fire whenever a triggered image appears, whereas prior deployment-triggered attacks activate only when model weights are quantized or pruned. However, conventional LVLM backdoors exhibit nearly 100% attack success rate (ASR) under full-token inference, immediately exposing compromised checkpoints during pre-deployment auditing. We reveal context stripping: surrounding clean visual tokens suppress an embedded trigger at full length, whereas token pruning strips this context away and activates the backdoor. Motivated by this finding, we propose StripWake, a projector-only backdoor that remains dormant under full-token auditing yet activates across unseen compressors. Specifically, StripWake pairs clean-supervised full-token views with target-supervised randomized compressed views, and aligns early visual attention with a frozen benign teacher to preserve clean utility. On LLaVA-1.5-7B across nine unseen compressors, StripWake stays dormant at 0.4% full-token ASR yet achieves 94.0%-99.7% compressed ASR across five primary compressors without CIDEr loss.

title: AdapBench: Adaptive Early-Stopping and Prioritization for Efficient Microbenchmarking in Cloud-based CI/CD
shortTitle: AdapBench: Adaptive Early-Stopping and Prioritization for Efficient Microbenchmarking in Cloud-based CI/CD
abstract: Cloud-based software systems frequently release new versions, a fact further accelerated through agentic coding. Each new release, however, brings the risk of performance regressions which can irritate end users, increase infrastructure costs, and increase carbon footprints. Therefore, developers strive to catch such regressions in testing stages, usually through so-called continuous benchmarking. The standard way of doing this is using microbenchmark suites which, however, take notoriously long to execute. Optimizing the execution of microbenchmark suites is, hence, an active field of research. In this paper, we propose AdapBench, an online scheduling system for reducing the execution duration of microbenchmark suites. AdapBench is the first approach which dynamically makes at-runtime decisions for prioritizing the most informative benchmarks and early-stopping each one once enough evidence has accumulated to accept or reject a performance change hypothesis. We evaluate our prototype on eight popular Java projects, commonly used by microbenchmark research, and four additional Go projects. At matched 90% change detections and false-positive rate compared to an optimistic uniform run, AdapBench saves 42% of the aggregate execution duration on the Java projects, with negligible scheduling overhead (below 0.001% of the total runtime). On the Go projects, AdapBench finds every performance change with zero false positives while saving 85% of the full run.

title: LoRAForge: Co-Designing Post-Hoc Compression and Execution for Efficient Multi-LoRA Serving
shortTitle: LoRAForge: Co-Designing Post-Hoc Compression and Execution for Efficient Multi-LoRA Serving
abstract: Multi-LoRA serving allows many task-specific adapters to share a common base model, but scaling to large adapter fleets introduces substantial storage, loading, and execution overheads. Post-hoc compression can reduce the memory footprint of trained LoRA adapters, yet smaller ranks do not automatically translate into faster serving. For instance, padding, factor access, and generic kernels can obscure the retained low-rank structure, while independently recompressing thousands of modules also incurs significant preparation overhead. We present LoRAForge, a system connecting batched factor construction to rank-specialized execution through an explicit retained-rank representation. It supports two allocation policies: uniform retention ratios (LoRAForge-U) and spectral-energy budget allocation (LoRAForge-S). Both share FlashTSQR factor construction and the same serving backend. FlashTSQR exploits parallelism across modules and row tiles, accelerating factor construction by up to $2.28\times$ over matched library QR. In a fixed-work Qwen control, the shared runtime adds $1.17$--$1.22\times$ throughput across both compressed policies, with negligible gains on original adapters. Across 85 trained open-weighted Qwen and Llama adapters, the spectral policy's floored quality configuration retains about 7.7% of adapter parameters with fleet-average score drops of at most 1.2 points on a 0--100 scale. The same rank-floored $1/12$ spectral exports achieve substantial token-throughput gains on both AMD and NVIDIA GPUs.

title: MedAstra: ASR-less Speech Retrieval with Diagnostic Grounding for Medical QA
shortTitle: MedAstra: ASR-less Speech Retrieval with Diagnostic Grounding for Medical QA
abstract: Spoken medical question answering can fail when automatic speech recognition (ASR) corrupts a clinically important term before retrieval. We present MedAstra, a framework that maps frozen WavLM speech representations through a lightweight adapter into a frozen E5 text embedding space. This enables a dense retrieval path that accepts a waveform without a query transcript. Retrieved passages and speech-linked textual metadata support answer generation with entity alternatives, diagnostic contrasts, relation heuristics, and bounded retrieval refinement. ASR-less refers to the initial speech retrieval interface; lexical retrieval, string-based entity correction, and the text generator require textual inputs. The deterministic speech embedding does not constitute a calibrated model of acoustic uncertainty. Reported retrieval results reach 87.6 Recall@10 for the speech-only retriever and 90.4 for the hybrid configuration, compared with 81.0 for transcript-first dense retrieval. Medical QA and ablations provide descriptive system comparisons, with input-provenance and evaluation limitations stated explicitly. We distinguish controlled synthetic acoustic tests from real clinical speech, qualify component attribution, and specify the remaining comparisons needed to assess speech-only QA and clinical generalization.

title: Does Random Search Discover Task Experts? Revisiting Neural Thickets
shortTitle: Does Random Search Discover Task Experts? Revisiting Neural Thickets
abstract: Pretrained models are typically viewed as generalists, requiring bespoke post-training to achieve task-specific expertise. Gan & Isola (2026) recently proposed a striking alternative: that pretrained models lie in a dense neural thicket of task specialists, which can be surfaced with simple Gaussian weight perturbations. We examine this neural thicket of task-specific experts and identify several key findings that question this perspective. First, we find that the apparent lift of the best-of-N selected perturbation decays quickly with selection-set size m, strongly suggesting overfitting to the selection questions. In fact, for 10 of the 12 model-task pairs we study, a simple null model of pure selection noise predicts more than 75 percent of the top expert's reward lift. Second, the top experts' advantage often vanishes on held-out questions or remains within the run-to-run variability of the unperturbed pretrained model. Third, we find that majority voting over the top-K selected perturbations, termed RandOpt(N, K) by Gan & Isola (2026), is often matched or outperformed by majority voting over K samples from the base model. Overall, our results suggest that random weight perturbations may be ineffective at uncovering task experts around pretrained models, and that task adaptation requires more sophistication than random search. Code and artifacts are available at github.com/asil012/RevisitingNeuralThickets.

title: StreamClarify: Proactive Clarification for Grounded Streaming Video Question Answering
shortTitle: StreamClarify: Proactive Clarification for Grounded Streaming Video Question Answering
abstract: Streaming video question answering (QA) requires real-time reasoning over continuous video streams under strict latency and active-context budgets. Current streaming vision-language models (VLMs) often give confident yet ungrounded answers when queries are ambiguous or have false premises, or when relevant visual evidence is no longer in the active context. Proactive clarification can help, but must satisfy the same latency and memory constraints. We present StreamClarify, a training-free framework for grounded streaming QA that combines a pre-answer uncertainty check with hierarchical memory. The check uses the entropy of a binary pre-answer judgment as a lightweight uncertainty score to decide whether to answer directly or request clarification. To support re-answering, a temporal-pyramid KV cache maintains a bounded active visual context, while a CPU-side semantic retrieval archive provides access to historical frames. We further construct StreamClarify-QA, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,837 QA pairs from StreamBench and OVO-Bench, spanning standard, referential ambiguity, and unanswerable scenarios. Across three VLM backbones, StreamClarify improves Macro accuracy by up to 8.2 points over backbone-matched baselines. At comparable trigger rates, entropy-based selection achieves more than 18 points higher precision than random selection in identifying initially incorrect answers. Under oracle user guidance, clarification improves Macro accuracy by up to 3.5 points. We also report a controlled, oracle-assisted Qwen3-VL simulation on Ambiguous QA with generated questions and referent-only user replies, where the entropy-gated condition improves accuracy by 8.3 points.

title: EZ-Ar-VC: Robust Arabic Voice Anonymization with Generalization across Dialects and Code-Switching
shortTitle: EZ-Ar-VC: Robust Arabic Voice Anonymization with Generalization across Dialects and Code-Switching
abstract: Voice conversion (VC) models can be used to anonymize speech data while preserving naturalness. Existing models, however, are mainly optimized for English and other high-resource languages, and they fail to generalize well to Arabic due to its distinct phonology. In this work, we comprehensively evaluate existing zero-shot VC systems for Arabic speech, identifying limitations in pronunciation preservation. We then train an Arabic-centric model based on EZ-VC on diverse Arabic speech, and demonstrate strong performance in intelligibility, naturalness, and pronunciation preservation, while maintaining high speaker dissimilarity. Through subjective evaluation, we further demonstrate its robustness to code-switching and cross-dialectal conversion, as well as its generalization to Arabic dialects with limited representation in the training data. Our findings highlight the limitations of zero-shot VC and the importance of target-language adaptation for robust voice anonymization.

title: Learning momenta for Hamiltonian-based models
shortTitle: Learning momenta for Hamiltonian-based models
abstract: There has been increasing interest in methodologies that incorporate physics priors into neural network architectures to enhance their modeling capabilities. Among these methodologies, Hamiltonian neural networks (HNNs) and their variants have gained considerable attention. These architectures explicitly encode Hamiltonian mechanics both in their structure and loss function, resulting in desirable properties and additional modeled information. A crucial limitation of HNNs is their reliance on data on the target system's generalized momenta. This severely hampers their applicability when the analytical form of the generalized momenta is unknown, which frequently is the case in real-world applications. The goal of the present work is to develop a general extension of Hamiltonian-based architectures that addresses this issue by simultaneously learning the system's generalized momenta, Hamiltonian structure, and dynamics from data. The proposed architecture learns the generalized momenta when their analytical form is unknown, and only (potentially non-sequential) data on the state and its derivatives is available. A dissipative mass-spring system, a double pendulum, and a rolling disk under nonholonomic constraints are considered as canonical examples to assess the performance of the proposed architecture.

title: Geometry of Confabulation and Refusal in Small Language Models
shortTitle: Geometry of Confabulation and Refusal in Small Language Models
abstract: Faced with an unanswerable question, small language models can either refuse or confabulate: confidently produce a wrong answer. Can the hidden state before the first generated token provide a clue? Can we flip confabulations into refusals? I introduce ConfabQA, a 784-item benchmark whose obscure-pre-cutoff category breaks the typical correctness/knowledge-cutoff confound and map the geometry of the hidden state with linear probes, a sparse autoencoder (SAE), and direct optimization of intervention directions. On Qwen3-1.7B and Gemma 2 2B the probe separates upcoming refusals from confabulations well beyond prompt features (+7.4/+16.3 pp); on Llama 3.2 3B the ConfabQA margin is within fold-to-fold spread, but a direct refusal probe on PopQA and TriviaQA recovers +18-25 pp. On Qwen I closely inspect three candidate directions for the refusal vector: probe-recovered, Qwen-Scope SAE feature, and directly optimized. Although the three directions are pairwise 50-81 degrees apart, a push at or below the state's own norm along any of them flips most confabulations into refusal openings dominated by the "As..." family. Forcing the opener without touching the hidden state yields the same one-in-three judged-refusal rate as any push. The opposite push collapses refusals mostly into confabulations, yet leaves originally correct answers intact, so the direction gates the opening speech act rather than the knowledge behind it. Confabulations do not resolve into a concentrated feature in a dictionary or a token signature on Qwen3-1.7B. Scoring every probe on the margin over the strongest of four prompt-feature baselines extracts the hidden state's own contribution. Correctness signal is model-dependent and portable only for Llama 3.2 3B: 81% of the probe's margin over test majority survives transfer between ConfabQA, PopQA, and TriviaQA. title: OntoDoc: Automatically Generating Ontology Resource Descriptions
shortTitle: OntoDoc: Automatically Generating Ontology Resource Descriptions
abstract: Knowledge graphs and ontologies form the backbone of structured, machine-readable knowledge representation, yet ontology terms often lack natural language descriptions, limiting their accessibility and reuse. Existing ontology verbalization approaches tend to rely on rule-based or template-driven techniques that operate on strict, formal schema axioms, resulting in rigid verbalizations that fail to convey richer contextual semantics. We present OntoDoc, a multi-agent framework for automatically generating natural language descriptions for any Internationalized Resource Identifier (IRI) within a SPARQL endpoint or RDF file. OntoDoc operates through a four-stage pipeline: (1) a Database Context agent that adaptively explores the knowledge graph via SPARQL to collect semantically informative triples about the target IRI; (2) a Web Context agent that retrieves and re-ranks encyclopedic background knowledge from Wikipedia and the open web; (3) an Assumption Generation agent that synthesizes both contexts into a structured, evidence-grounded list of intermediate assumptions; and (4) a Description Generation agent that produces the final natural language description from the grounded assumptions. We evaluate OntoDoc on three knowledge graphs spanning biomedical, agricultural, and cross-domain settings, using both automatic scoring via Large Language Models (LLMs) and human evaluation with 11 annotators. OntoDoc consistently matches or exceeds a naive LLM baseline and a template-based ontology verbalizer in accuracy. Furthermore, it vastly outperforms both baselines in the completeness of the generated descriptions, delivering an average 12% improvement in completeness over the naive baseline across all domains, and improving completeness scores by as much as 2.8 points on a 5-point scale relative to the ontology verbalizer.
